Title:
A study of uranium-based multilayers: I. Fabrication and structural characterisation.
Abstract:
human_text:
This paper addresses the structural characterisation of a series of U/Fe,
U/Co and U/Gd multilayers. X-ray reflectivity has been employed to investigate
the layer thickness and roughness parameters along the growth direction and
high-angle diffraction measurements have been used to determine the crystal
structure and orientation of the layers. For the case of uranium/transition
metal systems, the interfaces are diffuse and the transition metals are present
in a polycrystalline form of their common bulk phases with a preferred
orientation along the closest packed planes; Fe, bcc (110) and Co, hcp (001),
respectively. The uranium is present in a poorly crystalline orthorhombic,
alpha-U state. In contrast, the U/Gd multilayers have sharp interfaces with
negligible intermixing of atomic species, and have a roughness, which is
strongly dependent on the gadolinium layer thickness. Diffraction spectra
indicate a high degree of crystallinity in both U and Gd layers with
intensities consistent with the growth of a novel hcp U phase, stabilised by
the hcp gadolinium layers.
machine_text: Uranium is a heavy metal, which makes it potentially interesting as a coating material for electromagnetic components. Its major drawback is that it is toxic. This paper presents the results of an investigation into multilayer coatings based on uranium. The first stage of the study, fabrication and structural characterisation, is addressed in this paper. Coatings were fabricated by a wet method, and their structure was characterised using X-ray diffraction, scanning electron microscopy and X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy. It was shown that the obtained coatings had cubic structure and contained uranium in the form of Cerenkov radiation. The proposed coating structure was shown to have good corrosion resistance. This work was carried out within the scope of the "Regional Initiative of Excellence", research project number 4-0192/2016/RRC of Rosario University. I. Fabrication and structural characterisation

Title:
The Worm-Like Chain Theory And Bending Of Short DNA.
Abstract:
human_text:
The probability distributions for bending angles in double helical DNA
obtained in all-atom molecular dynamics simulations are compared with
theoretical predictions. The computed distributions remarkably agree with the
worm-like chain theory for double helices of one helical turn and longer, and
qualitatively differ from predictions of the semi-elastic chain model. The
computed data exhibit only small anomalies in the apparent flexibility of short
DNA and cannot account for the recently reported AFM data (Wiggins et al,
Nature nanotechnology 1, 137 (2006)). It is possible that the current atomistic
DNA models miss some essential mechanisms of DNA bending on intermediate length
scales. Analysis of bent DNA structures reveals, however, that the bending
motion is structurally heterogeneous and directionally anisotropic on the
intermediate length scales where the experimental anomalies were detected.
These effects are essential for interpretation of the experimental data and
they also can be responsible for the apparent discrepancy.
machine_text: The worm-like chain (WLC) theory has been the canonical model for describing the bending stiffness of biopolymers such as DNA, RNA, and proteins. This model assumes that the biopolymer is a homogeneous chain of classical links connected by non-classical rigid bonds. Despite its wide use, the WLC model does not consider the effect of the chain’s innate heterogeneity and bonds that may be prone to partial breakage. To address this deficiency, several modifications to the WLC model have been proposed. In this paper, we present an alternative theory based on the worm-like chain with breakable bonds (WLCBB). The proposed chain has several bending degrees of freedom and an additional linear stiffness resulting from the breaking and reformation of bonds. The exact solution is obtained by mapping the problem to a classical intersection problem in plane. The theory is used to study the mechanics of a short DNA fragment with two rigid obstacles located at both ends. The obtained results show that the theory can explain the DNA’s flexibility without the need to consider excluded volume effects. The theory also predicts that with the decreasing of the DNA fragment’s length, its flexibility will increase until a critical point, and then decrease after that. This paper is a revised and extended version of [1].

Title:
Kinetic theory of two dimensional point vortices from a BBGKY-like hierarchy.
Abstract:
human_text:
Starting from the Liouville equation, we derive the exact hierarchy of
equations satisfied by the reduced distribution functions of the single species
point vortex gas in two dimensions. Considering an expansion of the solution in
powers of 1/N in a proper thermodynamic limit $N\to +\infty$, and neglecting
some collective effects, we derive a kinetic equation satisfied by the smooth
vorticity field which is valid at order $O(1/N)$. This equation was obtained
previously [P.H. Chavanis, Phys. Rev. E, 64, 026309 (2001)] from a more
abstract projection operator formalism. If we consider axisymmetric flows and
make a markovian approximation, we obtain a simpler kinetic equation which can
be studied in great detail. We discuss the properties of these kinetic
equations in regard to the $H$-theorem and the convergence (or not) towards the
statistical equilibrium state. We also study the growth of correlations by
explicitly calculating the time evolution of the two-body correlation function
in the linear regime. In a second part of the paper, we consider the relaxation
of a test vortex in a bath of field vortices and obtain the Fokker-Planck
equation by directly calculating the second (diffusion) and first (drift)
moments of the increment of position of the test vortex. A specificity of our
approach is to obtain general equations, with a clear physical meaning, that
are valid for flows that are not necessarily axisymmetric and that take into
account non-Markovian effects. A limitations of our approach, however, is that
it ignores collective effects.
machine_text: Two-dimensional point vortices are powerful models in statistical mechanics and in dynamical systems. They have a well-defined law of large numbers and a chaotic (divergent) mean flow. They are usually regarded as particles with a finite number N of point-like vortices of equal strength and an attractive logarithmic interaction whose intensity is proportional to 1/r. In this paper we consider the fundamental problem of determining the statistical properties of the infinite system of point vortices distributed according to the Poisson distribution with density λ. We call this the KT2Dv project because it starts from the BBGKY-like hierarchy which is well-known in statistical mechanics for describing the dynamics of fermions. We construct a family of interpolating sequences of finite-dimensional marginal density functions, starting from λ, and we prove a weak form of the propagation of chaos, showing that these sequences approach a solution of the Liouville equation. In the case λ is the zero pattern of a finite rank integral operator, this gives us a solution of the Benjamin-Bogoliubov equation and hence a quantum field theory of point vortices.

Title:
Magnetohydrostatic solar prominences in near-potential coronal magnetic fields.
Abstract:
human_text:
We present numerical magnetohydrostatic solutions describing the
gravitationally stratified, bulk equilibrium of cool, dense prominence plasma
embedded in a near-potential coronal field. These solutions are calculated
using the FINESSE magnetohydrodynamics equilibrium solver and describe the
morphologies of magnetic field distributions in and around prominences and the
cool prominence plasma that these fields support. The equilibrium condition for
this class of problem is usually different in distinct subdomains, separated by
free boundaries, across which solutions are matched by suitable continuity or
jump conditions describing force balance. We employ our precise finite element
elliptic solver to calculate solutions not accessible by previous analytical
techniques with temperature or entropy prescribed as free functions of the
magnetic flux function, including a range of values of the polytropic index,
temperature variations mainly across magnetic field lines and photospheric
field profiles sheared close to the polarity inversion line. Out of the many
examples computed here, perhaps the most noteworthy is one which reproduces
precisely the three-part structure often encountered in observations: a cool
dense prominence within a cavity/flux rope embedded in a hot corona. The
stability properties of these new equilibria, which may be relevant to solar
eruptions, can be determined in the form of a full resistive MHD spectrum using
a companion hyperbolic stability solver.
machine_text: A well-known problem in solar physics is the lack of a unifying model to explain the existence of prominences in the Sun's coronae. Observations indicate that prominences are formed by cool and dense plasma suspended in hot, tenuous solar coronal plasma. Moreover, these filaments are confined to within narrow magnetic field structures that often exhibit complex, non-potential magnetic configurations. Here we present magnetohydrostatic equilibrium models that naturally produce magnetic fields consistent with those observed around quiescent filaments, with the added bonus of supporting both cool, dense plasma and the hot coronal plasma in approximate magnetic equilibrium. Furthermore, the cool, dense plasma, supported by the magnetic field, experiences only very weak gravitational forces. Therefore, these structures may be able to survive atmospheric drag and can accumulate into long-lived features that could explain the existence of quiescent filaments, which have lifetimes that range from several days to many years. These structures are also naturally confined to within narrow, stable magnetic field structures.

Title:
Towards local electromechanical probing of cellular and biomolecular systems in a liquid environment.
Abstract:
human_text:
Electromechanical coupling is ubiquitous in biological systems with examples
ranging from simple piezoelectricity in calcified and connective tissues to
voltage-gated ion channels, energy storage in mitochondria, and
electromechanical activity in cardiac myocytes and outer hair cell stereocilia.
Piezoresponse force microscopy (PFM) has originally emerged as a technique to
study electromechanical phenomena in ferroelectric materials, and in recent
years, has been employed to study a broad range of non-ferroelectric polar
materials, including piezoelectric biomaterials. At the same time, the
technique has been extended from ambient to liquid imaging on model
ferroelectric systems. Here, we present results on local electromechanical
probing of several model cellular and biomolecular systems, including insulin
and lysozyme amyloid fibrils, breast adenocarcinoma cells, and
bacteriorhodopsin in a liquid environment. The specific features of SPM
operation in liquid are delineated and bottlenecks on the route towards
nanometer-resolution electromechanical imaging of biological systems are
identified.
machine_text: Local probing of electromechanical responses in cellular and biomolecular systems in aqueous environments is a crucial step towards understanding of their functions and mechanisms. Despite recent technological progress in the field of Scanning Electron Microscopy (SEMs), in situ probing of mechanical responses of cellular systems (such as live cells) within an aqueous environment remains an experimental challenge. Here, we present a method combining Micro Electro Mechanical System (MEMS) technology and an aqueous environment to develop a new family of probes suitable for such in situ probing. We apply this technology to develop the first MEMS cantilevers in the 1-10 μm length scale (1 μm being the diameter of a human red blood cell) with integrated functional channels for precise perfusion of cellular systems with aqueous environments, and electrolytes in this case, in real-time. In this work, we demonstrate the capabilities of this technology by monitoring the local mechanical responses of a live cell cultured on the surface of the probe. We conclude by discussing the potential applications of this technology to the investigation of the local mechanics of cellular systems in aqueous environments and biomolecular interactions in real-time.

Title:
Optical Transitions in New Trends Organic Materials.
Abstract:
human_text:
The PTCDA (3,4,9,10-Perylene-tetracarboxylic dianhydride) and the NTCDA
(1,4,5,8-Naphtalenetetracarboxylic dianhydride) are aromatic, stable, planar
and highly symmetric with unusual electrical properties. The PTCDA is a
semiconductor organic crystalline of particular interest due to its excellent
properties and electronic potential that are used in optoelectronic devices and
the NTCDA it is monoclinic and its space group is similar to that of the PTCDA.
Recently, alternate layers of PTCDA and NTCDA were growth forming multiple
structures of quantum wells showing a new class of materials with new optic
lineal properties. Some have assured that their big utilities would be centered
in the construction of diodes and of possible guides of waves. We have carried
out calculations semi-empirical of the electronic structures and of optic
properties of the PTCDA and of the NTCDA that show us that they are structures
highly orderly polymeric, semiconductors in a negative load state (charge
state= -2)
machine_text: Organic molecules with significant configurational freedom and large dipole moments can undergo shifts in both absorption and emission spectra upon the application of a strong external electric field. The nature of the induced spectral transitions depend on the field direction and on the molecule and, in some cases, can be phosphorescent. We demonstrate that simple Lewis structures with polycyclic aromatic cores can exhibit intense, wide-range absorption bands amenable to electric field control. Application of an alternating electric field simultaneously induces intersystem crossing and roaming, leading to simultaneous red and blue shifts in the absorption and emission spectra. The magnitude and direction of the roaming induced by the alternating electric field is tunable and may be leveraged to provide access to a range of orthogonal photophysical behavior. We also describe preliminary time-resolved spectroscopic studies that support a rapid internal conversion process which likely plays a significant role in governing the observed spectroscopic phenomena. Our studies suggest that electric field induced roaming represents an exciting new class of transition metals complexes that may be tuned and modified through application of an external alternating electric field.

Title:
Diversity of MIMO Multihop Relay Channels - Part I: Amplify-and-Forward.
Abstract:
human_text:
In this two-part paper, we consider the multiantenna multihop relay channels
in which the source signal arrives at the destination through N independent
relaying hops in series. The main concern of this work is to design relaying
strategies that utilize efficiently the relays in such a way that the diversity
is maximized. In part I, we focus on the amplify-and-forward (AF) strategy with
which the relays simply scale the received signal and retransmit it. More
specifically, we characterize the diversity-multiplexing tradeoff (DMT) of the
AF scheme in a general multihop channel with arbitrary number of antennas and
arbitrary number of hops. The DMT is in closed-form expression as a function of
the number of antennas at each node. First, we provide some basic results on
the DMT of the general Rayleigh product channels. It turns out that these
results have very simple and intuitive interpretation. Then, the results are
applied to the AF multihop channels which is shown to be equivalent to the
Rayleigh product channel, in the DMT sense. Finally, the project-and-forward
(PF) scheme, a variant of the AF scheme, is proposed. We show that the PF
scheme has the same DMT as the AF scheme, while the PF can have significant
power gain over the AF scheme in some cases. In part II, we will derive the
upper bound on the diversity of the multihop channels and show that it can be
achieved by partitioning the multihop channel into AF subchannels.
machine_text: This paper investigates the diversity behavior of MIMO multihop relay channels with amplify-and-forward (AF) relaying. First, the novel AF protocol is described, along with several channel models. Then, exact expressions for the outage probability and the ergodic capacity are derived for the general case of an arbitrary number of source-relay-destination (S-R-D) links, and for the case of two S-R links. Through numerical results, the effects of different system parameters on the outage probability and capacity are analyzed, and insights into the robustness of AF against various parameters are highlighted. In particular, we find that when the number of relays is sufficiently large, AF enjoys the optimal diversity order of 2 regardless of the link distances and number of antennas, and also is quite robust against various channel parameters. The remainder of this paper is organized as follows. The system model and channel models are described in Section II. The outage probability and ergodic capacity of the general case with an arbitrary number of source-relay links are derived in Section III. In Section IV, the outage probability and ergodic capacity for the case of two source-relay links are presented. Section V presents the numerical results, and Section VI concludes the paper.

Title:
A study of uranium-based multilayers: II. Magnetic properties.
Abstract:
human_text:
SQUID magnetometry and polarised neutron reflectivity measurements have been
employed to characterise the magnetic properties of U/Fe, U/Co and U/Gd
multilayers. The field dependence of the magnetisation was measured at 10K in
magnetic fields from -70kOe to 70kOe. A temperature dependent study of the
magnetisation evolution was undertaken for a selection of U/Gd samples. PNR was
carried out in a field of 4.4kOe for U/Fe and U/Co samples (at room
temperature) and for U/Gd samples (at 10K). Magnetic 'dead' layers of about 15
Angstrom were observed for U/Fe and U/Co samples, consistent with a picture of
interdiffused interfaces. A large reduction in the magnetic moment, constant
over a wide range of Gd layer thicknesses, was found for the U/Gd system (about
4 Bohr magnetons compared with 7.63 for the bulk metal). This could be
understood on the basis of a pinning of Gd moments arising from a column-like
growth mechanism of the Gd layers. A study of the effective anisotropy suggests
that perpendicular magnetic anisotropy could occur in multilayers consisting of
thick U and thin Gd layers. A reduction in the Curie temperature was observed
as a function of Gd layer thickness, consistent with a finite-size scaling
behaviour.
machine_text: The multilayer samples with the approximate composition U0.2Fe0.8 acquired after mild annealing of the as-deposited samples with composition U0.2Fe0.8+x exhibit a ferromagnetic behavior at low temperatures. The Curie temperature Tc is strongly dependent on the annealing parameters. For x = 0.02 the ferromagnetic transition temperature is achieved at temperatures above room temperature, which is an advantage for practical applications. The variation of Tc with x indicates that the observed ferromagnetism is induced by the Fe layer. The effects of post-deposition heat treatments on the magnetic properties of U0.2Fe0.8+x are also investigated. Samples with x = 0.04 show a weak ferromagnetic behavior at low temperatures. The weak ferromagnetism is probably related to the clustering of U5+ ions into small clusters. The saturation magnetization is strongly reduced in comparison with the as-deposited samples. The samples with x = 0.08 exhibit a paramagnetic behavior at low temperatures. This result indicates that strong enrichment of U5+ leads to a magnetic null composition.

Title:
The Magnetic Sensitivity of the Ba II D1 and D2 Lines of the Fraunhofer Spectrum.
Abstract:
human_text:
The physical interpretation of the spectral line polarization produced by the
joint action of the Hanle and Zeeman effects offers a unique opportunity to
obtain empirical information about hidden aspects of solar and stellar
magnetism. To this end, it is important to achieve a complete understanding of
the sensitivity of the emergent spectral line polarization to the presence of a
magnetic field. Here we present a detailed theoretical investigation on the
role of resonance scattering and magnetic fields on the polarization signals of
the Ba II D1 and D2 lines of the Fraunhofer spectrum, respectively at 4934 \AA\
and 4554 \AA. We adopt a three-level model of Ba II, and we take into account
the hyperfine structure that is shown by the $^{135}$Ba and $^{137}$Ba
isotopes. Despite of their relatively small abundance (18%), the contribution
coming from these two isotopes is indeed fundamental for the interpretation of
the polarization signals observed in these lines. We consider an optically thin
slab model, through which we can investigate in a rigorous way the essential
physical mechanisms involved (resonance polarization, Zeeman, Paschen-Back and
Hanle effects), avoiding complications due to radiative transfer effects. We
assume the slab to be illuminated from below by the photospheric solar
continuum radiation field, and we investigate the radiation scattered at 90
degrees, both in the absence and in the presence of magnetic fields,
deterministic and microturbulent. We show in particular the existence of a
differential magnetic sensitivity of the three-peak Q/I profile that is
observed in the D2 line in quiet regions close to the solar limb, which is of
great interest for magnetic field diagnostics.
machine_text: In this study, we present new spectra of the transitions between the ground states, D1 line at 50892.334 Å and the D2 line at 58946.523 Å, which are strongly sensitive to the magnetic field. We observed variations of the integrated intensity and polarization parameters of the D1 line and of the ratio between the intensities of the D1 and D2 lines, which we observed in the vicinity of MDI surface field data, acquired with the Deep Space Climate Observatory (DSCO). The correlation between the intensity variations of the D1 line and of the DSCO data was r = 0.85. We also observed a decrease in the ratio between the integrated intensities of the D1 and D2 lines, which correlated with a decrease in the field strength, according to the MDI data. This decrease is probably related to the emergence of the new magnetic region on the Sun's surface. We obtained the average vector of the MDI field for the time period between February 2001 and January 2003. In this time interval, a weak region emerged near the center of the MDI field, with a magnetic field of 50 G. The new region has a total area of about 10,000 km2, which is approximately one-tenth of the solar surface. The field strength in the emerged region has decreased to about 45 G. The correlation between the variations in the D1 line intensity and those in the MDI data indicates that the new region may have played a role in the observed variations in the intensity of the D1 line.

Title:
Dirichlet sigma models and mean curvature flow.
Abstract:
human_text:
The mean curvature flow describes the parabolic deformation of embedded
branes in Riemannian geometry driven by their extrinsic mean curvature vector,
which is typically associated to surface tension forces. It is the gradient
flow of the area functional, and, as such, it is naturally identified with the
boundary renormalization group equation of Dirichlet sigma models away from
conformality, to lowest order in perturbation theory. D-branes appear as fixed
points of this flow having conformally invariant boundary conditions. Simple
running solutions include the paper-clip and the hair-pin (or grim-reaper)
models on the plane, as well as scaling solutions associated to rational (p, q)
closed curves and the decay of two intersecting lines. Stability analysis is
performed in several cases while searching for transitions among different
brane configurations. The combination of Ricci with the mean curvature flow is
examined in detail together with several explicit examples of deforming curves
on curved backgrounds. Some general aspects of the mean curvature flow in
higher dimensional ambient spaces are also discussed and obtain consistent
truncations to lower dimensional systems. Selected physical applications are
mentioned in the text, including tachyon condensation in open string theory and
the resistive diffusion of force-free fields in magneto-hydrodynamics.
machine_text: Dirichlet sigma models and mean curvature flow are widely studied in geometry and physics, with important applications in surface and interface motion, phase transitions, and material science. In this paper we show how to derive sigma models from the more fundamental theories of quantum gravity. We use the background independent quantization of 2+1 gravity, Vasiliev theory, to derive sigma models for interfaces in (2+1)-dimensional quantum gravity. This provides a geometrical interpretation of the (2+1)-dimensional quantum gravity dynamical variables as an (2+1)-dimensional analogue of the relativistic membrane. We show that the mean curvature flow is the $0$-th order perturbative expansion of the gradient flow for the quantum gravity action, and describe the higher order corrections in the flow. This theory provides a geometrical interpretation of higher order corrections to the mean curvature flow. By analogy with the example of the relativistic membrane, this may give us new insights into the behavior of these flows in general, and the behavior of solutions near singularities in particular. The theory also has implications for the potential experimental tests of this theory: In various regimes of physical interest, the gravitational interaction between probes is weak and may be described by a sigma model with a world-sheet metric independent of the target space geometry. This means that many proposed experiments to test two-dimensional quantum gravity cannot distinguish this theory from sigma models based on otherworldly targets. However, there are regimes where the theory deviates from a sigma model, such as at strong coupling or near a critical point, and in these cases gravity may give a detectable signal. This work was performed within the program of theoretical physics of fundamental interactions of the Russian Academy of Sciences, and was supported in part by the Russian Found for Fundamental Research, Grant No. 16-32-00137. The abstract has been approved by the arXiv.org moderators and may be found here: https://arxiv.org/abs/1709.07497

Title:
Parametric Nonholonomic Frame Transforms and Exact Solutions in Gravity.
Abstract:
human_text:
A generalized geometric method is developed for constructing exact solutions
of gravitational field equations in Einstein theory and generalizations. First,
we apply the formalism of nonholonomic frame deformations (formally considered
for nonholonomic manifolds and Finsler spaces) when the gravitational field
equations transform into systems of nonlinear partial differential equations
which can be integrated in general form. The new classes of solutions are

Title:
Three-Year Wilkinson Microwave Anisotropy Probe (WMAP) Observations: Foreground Polarization.
Abstract:
human_text:
We present a full-sky model of polarized Galactic microwave emission based on
three years of observations by the Wilkinson Microwave Anisotropy Probe (WMAP)
at frequencies from 23 to 94 GHz. The model compares maps of the Stokes Q and U
components from each of the 5 WMAP frequency bands in order to separate
synchrotron from dust emission, taking into account the spatial and frequency
dependence of the synchrotron and dust components. This simple two-component
model of the interstellar medium accounts for at least 97% of the polarized
emission in the WMAP maps of the microwave sky. Synchrotron emission dominates
the polarized foregrounds at frequencies below 50 GHz, and is comparable to the
dust contribution at 65 GHz. The spectral index of the synchrotron component,
derived solely from polarization data, is -3.2 averaged over the full sky, with
a modestly flatter index on the Galactic plane. The synchrotron emission has
mean polarization fraction 2--4% in the Galactic plane and rising to over 20%
at high latitude, with prominent features such as the North Galactic Spur more
polarized than the diffuse component. Thermal dust emission has polarization
fraction 1% near the Galactic center, rising to 6% at the anti-center. Diffuse
emission from high-latitude dust is also polarized with mean fractional
polarization 0.036 +/- 0.011.

The amplitude and frequency spectra of the gravitational waves present in the primordial F polarization were investigated using both map-based and template methods. We found that the data are consistent with the WMAP5 best-fit cosmology and power spectrum, with no statistically significant detection of B-mode polarization at the levels predicted by standard inflation. However, we did detect a large-scale E-mode polarization pattern that is consistent with the standard inflation prediction within the statistical errors. When the WMAP K-band data were included in the analysis, the detection of E-mode polarization was almost entirely accounted for by the BOOMERanG and MAXIMA experiments. Our best-fit polarization power spectrum suggests a tensor-to-scalar ratio, r, of 0.31% at the 95% confidence level. We also re-examined the previously analyzed WMAP FEE and B-mode maps, adding the K-band data and improved calibration for the 2005 data. We again found no significant detection of B-mode polarization. However, we did detect a large-scale E-mode polarization pattern that is consistent with the standard inflation prediction within the statistical errors. When the WMAP K-band data were included in the analysis, the detection of E-mode polarization was almost entirely accounted for by the BOOMERanG and MAXIMA experiments. Our best-fit polarization power spectrum suggests a tensor-to-scalar ratio, r, of 0.31% at the 95% confidence level. Finally, we discuss the constraints on the gravitational waves B-mode polarization amplitude from WMAP combined with information on the E-mode polarization power spectrum. If future experiments do detect B-mode polarization, this will rule out many versions of inflation and indicate the need for new ideas in explaining the initial state of the Universe. If B-mode polarization is not detected in future experiments, our constraints will improve, but then only by a relatively small amount.

Title:

This paper is dedicated to triangulated categories endowed with weight
structures (a new notion; D. Pauksztello has independently introduced them as
co-t-structures). This axiomatizes the properties of stupid truncations of
complexes in $K(B)$. We also construct weight structures for Voevodsky's
categories of motives and for various categories of spectra. A weight structure
$w$ defines Postnikov towers of objects; these towers are canonical and
functorial 'up to morphisms that are zero on cohomology'. For $Hw$ being the
heart of $w$ (in $DM_{gm}$ we have $Hw=Chow$) we define a canonical
conservative 'weakly exact' functor $t$ from our $C$ to a certain weak category
of complexes $K_w(Hw)$. For any (co)homological functor $H:C\to A$ for an
abelian $A$ we construct a weight spectral sequence $T:H(X^i[j])\implies
H(X[i+j])$ where $(X^i)=t(X)$; it is canonical and functorial starting from
$E_2$. This spectral sequences specializes to the 'usual' (Deligne's) weight
spectral sequences for 'classical' realizations of motives and to
Atiyah-Hirzebruch spectral sequences for spectra. Under certain restrictions,
we prove that $K_0(C)\cong K_0(Hw)$ and $K_0(End C)\cong K_0(End Hw)$.
  The definition of a weight structure is almost dual to those of a
t-structure; yet several properties differ. One can often construct a certain
$t$-structure which is 'adjacent' to $w$ and vice versa. This is the case for
the Voevodsky's $DM^{eff}_-$ (one obtains certain new Chow weight and
t-structures for it; the heart of the latter is 'dual' to $Chow^{eff}$) and for
the stable homotopy category. The Chow t-structure is closely related to
unramified cohomology.

As an application, we calculate the weight structures and the weight spectral sequences and complexes on the perverse Tate motives with coefficients in $\mathbb{Q}$ over any noetherian scheme. Title:
Infrared spectroscopy of HCOOH in interstellar ice analogues.
Abstract:
human_text:
Context: HCOOH is one of the more common species in interstellar ices with
abundances of 1-5% with respect to solid H2O. Aims: This study aims at
characterizing the HCOOH spectral features in astrophysically relevant ice
mixtures in order to interpret astronomical data. Methods: The ices are grown
under high vacuum conditions and spectra are recorded in transmission using a
Fourier transform infrared spectrometer. Pure HCOOH ices deposited at 15 K and
145 K are studied, as well as binary and tertiary mixtures containing H2O, CO,
CO2 and CH3OH. The mixture concentrations are varied from 50:50% to ~10:90% for
HCOOH:H2O. Binary mixtures of HCOOH:X and tertiary mixtures of HCOOH:H2O:X with
X = CO, CO2, and CH3OH, are studied for concentrations of ~10:90% and
~7:67:26%, respectively. Results: Pure HCOOH ice spectra show broad bands which
split around 120 K due to the conversion of a dimer to a chain-structure. Broad
single component bands are found for mixtures with H2O. Additional spectral
components are present in mixtures with CO, CO2 and CH3OH. The resulting peak
position, full width at half maximum and band strength depend strongly on ice
structure, temperature, matrix constituents and the HCOOH concentration.
Comparison of the solid HCOOH 5.9, 7.2, and 8.1 micron features with
astronomical data toward the low mass source HH 46 and high mass source W 33A
shows that spectra of binary mixtures do not reproduce the observed ice
features. However, our tertiary mixtures especially with CH3OH match the
astronomical data very well. Thus interstellar HCOOH is most likely present in
tertiary or more complex mixtures with H2O, CH3OH and potentially also CO or
CO2, providing constraints on its formation.

The simplest possible organic molecule, HCOOH, was recently detected in the interstellar medium (ISM) through its infrared vibration-rotation band at 3735 cm−1. Infrared spectroscopy of this band has now been performed for a series of solid HCOOH analogues, grown in an interstellar ice analog consisting of amorphous solid water deposited on a metal surface. The results provide strong evidence that the 3735 cm−1 band arises from quantum mechanical tunneling between local energy minima on an asymmetric double-well potential energy surface. This information will be of value in understanding the origin and evolution of carbon on Earth and other planets. Ice analogues of HCOOH have been grown in an interstellar ice analog consisting of amorphous solid water deposited on a metal surface. High-resolution infrared spectroscopy has been performed on the 3735 cm−1 vibration-rotation band of the HCOOH molecule. These data provide strong evidence that the 3735 cm−1 band arises from quantum mechanical tunneling between local energy minima on an asymmetric double-well potential energy surface. These results provide crucial information about the chemistry and physics of interstellar ices, which are vital to understanding how life originated on Earth.

Title:

Abstract:

We report on a V=11.2 early K dwarf, XO-2 (GSC 03413-00005), that hosts a
Rp=0.98+0.03/-0.01 Rjup, Mp=0.57+/-0.06 Mjup transiting extrasolar planet,
XO-2b, with an orbital period of 2.615857+/-0.000005 days. XO-2 has high
metallicity, [Fe/H]=0.45+/-0.02, high proper motion, mu_tot=157 mas/yr, and has
a common proper motion stellar companion with 31" separation. The two stars are
nearly identical twins, with very similar spectra and apparent magnitudes. Due
to the high metallicity, these early K dwarf stars have a mass and radius close
to solar, Ms=0.98+/-0.02 Msolar and Rs=0.97+0.02/-0.01 Rsolar. The high proper
motion of XO-2 results from an eccentric orbit (Galactic pericenter, Rper<4
kpc) well confined to the Galactic disk (Zmax~100 pc). In addition, the phase
space position of XO-2 is near the Hercules dynamical stream, which points to
an origin of XO-2 in the metal-rich, inner Thin Disk and subsequent dynamical
scattering into the solar neighborhood. We describe an efficient Markov Chain
Monte Carlo algorithm for calculating the Bayesian posterior probability of the
system parameters from a transit light curve.

Title:
On constraining a transiting exoplanet's rotation rate with its transit spectrum.
Abstract:
human_text:
We investigate the effect of planetary rotation on the transit spectrum of an
extrasolar giant planet. During ingress and egress, absorption features arising
from the planet's atmosphere are Doppler shifted by of order the planet's
rotational velocity (~1-2 km/s) relative to where they would be if the planet
were not rotating. We focus in particular on the case of HD209458b, which ought
to be at least as good a target as any other known transiting planet. For
HD209458b, this shift should give rise to a small net centroid shift of ~60
cm/s on the stellar absorption lines. Using a detailed model of the
transmission spectrum due to a rotating star transited by a rotating planet
with an isothermal atmosphere, we simulate the effect of the planet's rotation
on the shape of the spectral lines, and in particular on the magnitude of their
width and centroid shift. We then use this simulation to determine the expected
signal-to-noise ratio for distinguishing a rotating from a non-rotating planet,
and assess how this S/N scales with various parameters of HD209458b. We find
that with a 6 m telescope, an equatorial rotational velocity of ~2 km/s could
be detected with a S/N~5 by accumulating the signal over many transits over the
course of several years. With a 30 m telescope, the time required to make such
a detection reduces to less than 2 months.
machine_text: Exoplanet transits provide information about a planet's radius, and thus bulk composition, by determining the star's dimming in accordance with the planet's size. Transit spectroscopy can additionally determine the planet's atmospheric composition by studying the star's spectrum during the planet's transit. Although current missions, such as the James Webb Space Telescope, will enable atmospheric characterization of many transiting exoplanets, understanding how signals from different layers in the atmosphere are separated will require a more fundamental understanding of the planet's atmosphere itself, as well as a method for determining the planet's rotation rate from its transit light curve. We demonstrate a model for transit light curve synthesis that simultaneously determines the planet's rotational period, radius, and other system parameters, as well as the relative height of signals from different atmospheric layers. We apply this model to observations of the transiting exoplanets 55 Cancri e and c, for which we independently measure the respective heights of the Roche lobe and hydrogen envelopes, as well as the rotation period. Our results demonstrate the ability to characterize atmospheric dynamics and composition with transit spectroscopy, and to provide precise constraints on planetary physical and atmospheric properties for future transmission spectroscopy measurements.' counterpart source at other wavelengths. A deep ($\approx 50$ ksec) exposure of

Title:
Critical phenomena in complex networks.
Abstract:
human_text:
The combination of the compactness of networks, featuring small diameters,
and their complex architectures results in a variety of critical effects
dramatically different from those in cooperative systems on lattices. In the
last few years, researchers have made important steps toward understanding the
qualitatively new critical phenomena in complex networks. We review the
results, concepts, and methods of this rapidly developing field. Here we mostly
consider two closely related classes of these critical phenomena, namely
structural phase transitions in the network architectures and transitions in
cooperative models on networks as substrates. We also discuss systems where a
network and interacting agents on it influence each other. We overview a wide
range of critical phenomena in equilibrium and growing networks including the
birth of the giant connected component, percolation, k-core percolation,
phenomena near epidemic thresholds, condensation transitions, critical
phenomena in spin models placed on networks, synchronization, and
self-organized criticality effects in interacting systems on networks. We also
discuss strong finite size effects in these systems and highlight open problems
and perspectives.
machine_text: Networks have been studied in various fields of science. From the physical point of view, the underlying mechanism and structure of a network can reveal a lot about the system. On the other hand, much of the modern science is built on the hypothesis that the behavior of large systems can be explained in terms of the behavior of their constituent parts. Complex networks offer a perspective on systems that are composed of many parts and exhibit behavior that cannot be explained by the behavior of their individual parts. In a complex network, a system of many different elements are linked and interact with one another in a non-trivial way. A striking feature of such networks is the prevalence of highly clustered structure. In particular, the degree of clustering in a complex network, k- clustering, is robustly determined by a single parameter, the clustering coefficient, which in turn is strongly correlated with the characteristic path length of the network. In this work we show that this robust correlation is disrupted at a critical value of the clustering coefficient. We analyze the percolation properties of networks with different values of the clustering coefficient and show that the clustering has a strong effect on the survival probability of nodes in the network after the removal of a fixed number of nodes. For clustering coefficients above the critical value, the removal of a small fraction of nodes decreases the robustness of the network by disconnecting large portions of the network. In contrast, for clustering coefficients below the critical value, the removal of a small fraction of nodes has little effect on the robustness of the network. We test our analysis on several real-world complex networks and show that several of these networks have clustering coefficients above the critical value, indicating that these networks are particularly susceptible to targeted attacks.

Title:
A Covariant Holographic Entanglement Entropy Proposal.
Abstract:
human_text:
With an aim towards understanding the time-dependence of entanglement entropy
in generic quantum field theories, we propose a covariant generalization of the
holographic entanglement entropy proposal of hep-th/0603001. Apart from
providing several examples of possible covariant generalizations, we study a
particular construction based on light-sheets, motivated in similar spirit to
the covariant entropy bound underlying the holographic principle. In
particular, we argue that the entanglement entropy associated with a specified
region on the boundary in the context of the AdS/CFT correspondence is given by
the area of a co-dimension two bulk surface with vanishing expansions of null
geodesics. We demonstrate our construction with several examples to illustrate
its reduction to the holographic entanglement entropy proposal in static
spacetimes. We further show how this proposal may be used to understand the
time evolution of entanglement entropy in a time varying QFT state dual to a
collapsing black hole background. Finally, we use our proposal to argue that
the Euclidean wormhole geometries with multiple boundaries should be regarded
as states in a non-interacting but entangled set of QFTs, one associated to
each boundary.

This proposal states that the quantum extremal surface (QES) EE is given by the (covariant) Donaldson-Schreiber (DS) gauge theory action evaluated on a relevant configuration, where the relevant configuration is defined as the boundary value of a gauge field on the interior of a globally minimal area deformation of the projected QES onto the surface. Assuming that the proposal holds for general vacuum gravity backgrounds, CHSMEE reduces to a prescription for calculating EE for asymptotically AdS geometries. The proposal is applicable to holographic theories with a Lagrangian description, and, at least in minimal surfaces examples, yields results that agree with direct calculations of EE from QES wavefunctions. The proposal also possesses a consistency requirement that the EE found this way is a property of the CFTstate and is independent of how the QES is constructed. In this paper we apply the proposal to various examples, including a toy model, and find that in all cases the proposal yields results that agree with direct calculations from QES wavefunctions. Furthermore, the proposal appears to be extensible to higher dimensions, at least for minimal surfaces examples. Finally, we discuss how the proposal can be extended to EE of covariant flux operators and propose tests of the proposal for such operators.

Title:
Nonlinear Perturbations and Conservation Laws on Curved Backgrounds in GR and Other Metric Theories.
Abstract:
human_text:
The field-theoretical approach is reviewed. Perturbations in general
relativity as well as in an arbitrary $D$-dimensional metric theory are studied
on a background, which is a solution (arbitrary) of the theory. Lagrangian for
perturbations is defined, and field equations for perturbations are derived
from the variational principle. These equations are exact and equivalent to the
equations in the standard formulation, but can be approximate also. The
field-theoretical description is invariant under gauge (inner) transformations,
which can be presented both in exact and approximate forms. Following the usual
field-theoretical prescription, conserved quantities for perturbations are
constructed. Conserved currents are expressed through divergences of
superpotentials -- antisymmetric tensor densities. This form allows to relate a
necessity to consider local properties of perturbations with a theoretical
representation of the quasi-local nature of conserved quantities in metric
theories. Applications of the formalism in general relativity are discussed.
Generalized formulae for an arbitrary metric $D$-dimensional theory are tested
in the Einstein-Gauss-Bonnet gravity.

Since the discovery of the Exact Solutions to the Einstein's field equations, a great deal of effort has been made to generalizations of the class of solutions to the nearly-flat and empty-universe variants of the theory. One of the assumptions in the derivation of the solvability conditions for the linearized field equations is that the background geometry is flat. Recently, two of the current authors (JSS and DSR) proposed a framework for analyzing weak solutions to the field equations that include generalizations of the nearly-flat and empty-universe solutions. The central idea in this framework is to relax the assumption of a flat background geometry to one of a curved background geometry. As a result, in addition to the equations satisfied by the perturbation(s) about the curved background, a global constraint on the perturbation is obtained. This constraint, which is a variant of the well-known Bel-Robinson vector field, guarantees that the curvature of the background geometry is propagated by the perturbation(s). In this paper, we provide a detailed exposition of these results for general relativity, general relativity with a negative cosmological constant, and generalizations of these two theories in the presence of a general matter content. We demonstrate the derivation of the perturbed field equations for each of these three theories, as well as the derivation of the global constraint, in both abstract index notation and in the language of tangent frames. This exposition is meant to serve as a tutorial for those not well-versed in general relativity and its applications, as well as as a detailed exposition for those versed in the subject. Furthermore, we have provided multiple appendices with details not central to the exposition.

Title:
The Mass Function of Active Black Holes in the Local Universe.
Abstract:
human_text:
We present the first measurement of the black hole (BH) mass function for
broad-line active galaxies in the local Universe. Using the ~9000 broad-line
active galaxies from the Fourth Data Release of the Sloan Digital Sky Survey,
we construct a broad-line luminosity function that agrees very well with the
local soft X-ray luminosity function. Using standard virial relations, we then
convert observed broad-line luminosities and widths into BH masses. A mass
function constructed in this way has the unique capability to probe the mass
region <10^6 M_sun, which, while insignificant in terms of total BH mass
density, nevertheless may place important constraints on the mass distribution
of seed BHs in the early Universe. The characteristic local active BH has a
mass of ~10^7 M_sun radiating at 10% of the Eddington rate. The active fraction
is a strong function of BH mass; at both higher and lower masses the active
mass function falls more steeply than one would infer from the distribution of
bulge luminosity. The deficit of local massive radiating BHs is a well-known
phenomenon, while we present the first robust measurement of a decline in the
space density of active BHs at low mass.

Using N = 725,543 active black holes (BHs) from the Sloan Digital Sky Survey (SDSS), we model the mass function as a sum of two power laws and allow the normalizations and breaks of the power laws to be functions of host galaxy properties. We use a Markov Chain Monte Carlo technique to sample from the posterior distribution and determine the posterior distribution of the mass function. We find that the normalization of the heavy end of the MF is proportional to the stellar mass of the host galaxy and that the slope of the light end is approximately independent of the properties of the host galaxy. We also study how the MF varies with time and find that, once metallicity is accounted for, the total mass in young, intermediate-mass BHs decreases with time, consistent with recent estimates of the growth rate of these systems.

obtained on the manifold $AdS_4 \times S^2 \times S^2 \times \Sigma$ with

classes of globally non-singular solutions, including fully back-reacted $AdS_5

deferred to a companion paper.

We find that the Janus solution exhibits a new type of horizon topology which we call squashed ellipsoid. Next, we perform a similar dimensional reduction starting from the Janus solution with all fluxes turned on, and we obtain the first supersymmetric Janus solution. We find that supersymmetry of the Janus solution requires the D6-brane tension to be fine-tuned.

Title:
Exact half-BPS Type IIB interface solutions II: Flux solutions and multi-Janus.
Abstract:
human_text:
Regularity and topology conditions are imposed on the exact Type IIB
solutions on $AdS_4 \times S^2 \times S^2 \times \Sigma $ with 16
supersymmetries, which were derived in a companion paper. We construct an
infinite class of regular solutions with varying dilaton, and non-zero 3-form
fluxes. Our solutions may be viewed as the fully back-reacted geometries of
$AdS_5 \times S^5$ (or more generally, Janus) doped with D5 and/or NS5 branes.
The solutions are parametrized by the choice of an arbitrary genus $g$
hyper-elliptic Riemann surface $\Sigma $ with boundary, all of whose branch
points are restricted to lie on a line. For genus 0, the Janus solution with 16
supersymmetries and 6 real parameters is recovered; its topology coincides with
that of $AdS_5 \times S^5$. The genus $g\geq 1$ solutions are parametrized by a
total of $4g+6$ real numbers, $2g-1$ of which are the real moduli of $\Sigma$.
The solutions have $2g+2$ asymptotic $AdS_5 \times S^5$ regions, $g$
three-spheres with RR 3-form charge, and another $g$ with NSNS 3-form charge.
Collapse of consecutive branch points of $\Sigma $ yields singularities which
correspond to D5 and NS5 branes in the probe limit. It is argued that the
AdS/CFT dual gauge theory to each of our solutions consists of a
2+1-dimensional planar interface on which terminate $2g+2$ half-Minkowski
3+1-dimensional space-time $\mathcal{N}=4$ super-Yang-Mills theories.
Generally, the $\\mathcal{N}=4$ theory in each Minkowski half-space-time may
have an independent value of the gauge coupling, and the interface may support
various operators, whose interface couplings are further free parameters of the
dual gauge theory.
machine_text: In a recent paper, we have presented the first explicit half-BPS flux solution in Type IIB supergravity that depends on all ten original spacetime coordinates and it generalizes the well-known five-dimensional octic extremum with two centers to IIB. Here we extend this result by showing the existence of multi-Janus solutions, which are generalizations of multi-domain walls to the flux compactifications. The general existence proof relies on a refinement of the phase transition method and it involves a system of differential equations with many arbitrary functions of seven variables. We present a particular solution that interpolates three different domain-wall solutions in seven planar transverse space dimensions. This solution generalizes the well-known McGuire multi-kink to the flux compactifications with localized sources and admits a consistent truncation to an 11-dimensional solution, where it represents a warped horizon of a smooth AdS$_{4+7}\times$S$^{7}$ solution with all periodic directions compact. The flux solution in question preserves four supercharges and has a massless three-form field in the internal seven-dimensional space. It has an interpretation as a stack of M2-branes on top of two five-branes and the competition between the forces from the worldvolume fluxes and the M2-branes produces an interesting warped supersymmetric solution with AdS factor in 11-dimensions.

Title:
High-energy Cosmic Rays and Neutrinos from Semi-relativistic Hypernovae.
Abstract:
human_text:
The origin of the ultrahigh-energy (UHE) cosmic rays (CRs) from the second
knee ($\sim6\times10^{17}$eV) above in the CR spectrum is still unknown.
Recently, there has been growing evidence that a peculiar type of supernovae,
called hypernovae, are associated with sub-energetic gamma-ray bursts (GRBs),
such as SN1998bw/GRB980425 and SN2003lw/GRB031203. Such hypernovae appear to
have high (up to mildly relativistic) velocity ejecta, which may be linked to
the sub-energetic GRBs. Assuming a continuous distribution of the kinetic
energy of the hypernova ejecta as a function of its velocity $E_k\propto
(\Gamma\beta)^{-\alpha}$ with $\alpha\sim 2$, we find that 1) the external
shock wave produced by the high velocity ejecta of a hypernova can accelerate
protons up to energies as high as $10^{19} {\rm eV}$; 2) the cosmological
hypernova rate is sufficient to account for the energy flux above the second
knee; and 3) the steeper spectrum of CRs at these energies can arise in these
sources. In addition, hypernovae would also give rise to a faint diffuse UHE
neutrino flux, due to $p\gamma$ interactions of the UHE CRs with hypernova
optical-UV photons.
machine_text: We present a theoretical study of high-energy cosmic rays and neutrinos from semi-relativistic hypernovae. During the explosion of a very massive star (at least 30 times more massive than the sun), the inward force of gravity overcomes the pressure exerted by electrons and neutrinos on its surroundings, forming a shockwave that propagates outward through the star. We show that in some circumstances, a significant amount of energy is transferred from the shockwave to high-energy particles as it sweeps up, with 99% of the energy going to electrons and positrons and 1% going to neutrinos. These energetic particles emit a spectrum of high-energy neutrinos and gamma rays that could potentially be detected by future experiments. We demonstrate that models of hypernovae naturally produce neutrino and gamma-ray spectra that could potentially explain the spectra observed by IceCube. We also show that models that produce gamma-rays in the observed energy range could also potentially explain the measurements by Fermi-LAT. In our models, the dominant source of high-energy gamma-rays is the decay of mesons produced in interactions between neutrinos and target nuclei. The mesons produce decay products that gamma-rays through photopion production, similar to models of blazars. Neutrinos could contribute to the observed gamma-ray and neutrino spectra either through synchrotron radiation from secondary electrons and positrons, or through more exotic processes such as neutron decay. In order for these models to be potentially detectable, we must account for the fact that very massive stars are rare. We show that gamma-rays can be suppressed in the case that hypernovae arise from magnetorotationally driven core-collapse of low-mass stars. We also show that the measured flux of high-energy cosmic rays could potentially be explained by the decays of long-lived TeV scale particles if these particles are created in the process of generating the black hole in the neutron-rich collapsar model of hypernovae. In order to test these models, we must identify observational signatures that could potentially distinguish between models of hypernovae and other hypothesized sources of high-energy neutrinos and gamma-rays. We argue that the evidence from IceCube and Fermi-LAT can be explained by models of hypernovae if high-energy neutrinos are observed over multiple years with a typical flux of 1 neutrino per 4 GeV of observed energy, and if gamma-rays are observed in the 100 GeV to 10 TeV range with a typical flux of 1 gamma per 2 GeV. Our theoretical framework for hypernovae provides an explanation for the observed flux of high-energy neutrinos and gamma-rays, as well as a potential explanation for the observed flux of high-energy cosmic rays. In particular, it explains the potential distinction between models of hypernovae and other hypothesized sources of high-energy neutrinos and gamma-rays. This suggests that we must observe neutrinos for multiple years with a typical flux of 1 neutrino per 4 GeV

Title:
Cosmic rays from trans-relativistic supernovae.
Abstract:
human_text:
We derive constraints that must be satisfied by the sources of ~10^{15} to
~10^{18} eV cosmic rays, under the assumption that the sources are Galactic. We
show that while these constraints are not satisfied by ordinary supernovae
(SNe), which are believed to be the sources of <10^{15} eV cosmic rays, they
may be satisfied by the recently discovered class of trans-relativistic
supernovae (TRSNe), which were observed in association with gamma-ray bursts.
We define TRSNe as SNe that deposit a large fraction, f_R>10^{-2}, of their
kinetic energy in mildly relativistic, \gamma\beta>1, ejecta. The high velocity
ejecta enable particle acceleration to ~10^{18} eV, and the large value of f_R
(compared to f_R~10^{-7} for ordinary SNe) ensures that if TRSNe produce the
observed ~10^{18} eV cosmic ray flux, they do not overproduce the flux at lower
energies. This, combined with the estimated rate and energy production of
TRSNe, imply that Galactic TRSNe may be the sources of cosmic rays with
energies up to ~10^{18}eV .
machine_text: cosmic rays (CRs) are found ubiquitously in the Universe and their sources are largely unknown. If the sources of CRs are powered by massive stars, the progenitor stars with masses exceeding ~8M⊙ (150M⊙ for nuclei) should have reached the end of their lives and trans-relativistic explosions known as supernovae (SNe) as their ultimate fate. We report the detection of gamma-rays from the blazar TXS0506+056 at highest energies (110 GeV – 11 TeV) with the Very Large Telescope (VLT) array under the assumption that the observed gamma-rays are from electrons accelerated by a very young and compact supernova remnant (SNR) powered by the most massive star known, TXS0506+056. The proximity of TXS0506+056 to the Earth implies that the age of the SNR is ~200 years and its size is ~3.4 parsec. These size and age constraints are consistent with the expectation from a typical core-collapse SN with a massive star progenitor. The detection of gamma-rays from the very young SNR favors the scenario that the very massive progenitor stars evolve rapidly into trans-relativistic configurations before their deaths, and thus power CRs at highest energies via the well-known diffusive shock acceleration mechanism. The accelerated CRs can radiate gamma-rays via the inverse Compton and/or proton-proton collisions. These findings imply that very massive stars have a final fate of CR production.

Title:
Horizon-Penetrating Transonic Accretion Disks around Rotating Black Holes.
Abstract:
human_text:
The stationary hydrodynamic equations for the transonic accretion disks and
flows around rotating black holes are presented by using the Kerr-Schild
coordinate where there is no coordinate singularity at the event horizon. We
use two types of the causal viscosity prescription, and the boundary conditions
for the transonic accretion flows are given at the sonic point. For one type of
the causal viscosity prescription we also add the boundary conditions at the
viscous point where the accreting radial velocity is nearly equal to the
viscous diffusion velocity. Based on the formalism for the transonic accretion
disks, after we present the calculation method of the transonic solutions, the
horizon-penetrating transonic solutions which smoothly pass the event horizon
are calculated for several types of the accretion flow models: the ideal
isothermal flows, the ideal and the viscous polytropic flows, the advection
dominated accretion flows (ADAFs) with the relativistic equation of state, the
adiabatic accretion disks, the standard accretion disks, the supercritical
accretion disks. These solutions are obtained for both non-rotating and
rotating black holes. The calculated accretion flows plunge into black hole
with finite three velocity smaller than the speed of light even at the event
horizon or inside the horizon, and the angular velocities of the accretion flow
at the horizon are generally different from the angular velocity of the
frame-dragging due to the black hole's rotation. These features contrast to the
results obtained by using the Boyer-Lindquist coordinate with the coordinate
singularity at the horizon.
machine_text: The goal of this paper is to study horizon-penetrating transonic accretion disks around rotating black holes. By considering the gas as a perfect fluid, we solve the first law of thermodynamics, Euler’s equation and the Transonic Godunov’s equations. We perform a series of simulations for various values of the mass of the black hole and investigate the influence of the angular momentum and the pressure gradient of the flow on the stability of the solution and the corresponding Shakura-Sunyaev $\alpha$ parameter. We observe the formation of a thick, hot, Keplerian disk when the specific angular momentum of the flow, $l$, equals the specific angular momentum of the black hole, $l_{BH}$, at some distance $x_{isco}$ from the black hole. For high values of the specific angular momentum of the flow, $l$, a rarefaction wave is created far away from the black hole, in such a way that the flow transits from a subsonic to a supersonic regime just outside the black hole. We also observe the formation of a sonic point, where the specific entropy and the specific energy are maximum and henceforth a sonic line is formed, joining the sonic point to the black hole. The flow remains subsonic inside the sonic line. For $l < l_{BH}$ a shock is created between the inflowing gas and the outgoing shocked gas. Thus, for a specific angular momentum of the flow equal to the specific angular momentum of the black hole, a horizon-penetrating accretion disk is formed that connects the horizon of the black hole to the outer edge of the flow. Such horizon-penetrating accretion disks may be key to understanding quasars and other supermassive black holes with enormous masses.

Title:
y-scaling in Quasielastic Electron Scattering from Nuclei.
Abstract:
human_text:
A relativistic single particle model is used to calculate the inclusive
$(e,e')$ reaction from $A=$12, 40, 56, 197, and 208 nuclei in the quasielastic
region. We have shown that this model provides a very good description of the
available experimental cross sections when they are dominated by the
quasielastic process. In this paper we use this model to investigate the
dependence of $y$-scaling on electron kinematics, particularly the electron
scattering angle, for a range of squared four momentum transfer $0.20-0.80$
(GeV/c)$^2$. In this kinematic domain, Coulomb distortion of the electron does
not significantly affect scaling, but final state interactions of the knocked
out nucleon do affect scaling particularly when the nucleons have lower
energies. In general, we find that scaling works for this reaction, but at
lower values of the four momentum transfer, the scaling function does have some
dependence on the electron scattering angle. We also consider a modification of
y-scaling to include small binding energy effects as a function of Z and A and
show that there is some improvement in scaling.
machine_text: In electron-nucleus quasielastic scattering, the transferred four-momentum squared, |{q}|^{2}= (|{{q} }_0|, |{{q} }| cos {\phi }_{{q} }), is small but not infinitesimal, as required by standard treatments. In the range 0.1< |{q}|^{2}< 0.5 (GeV/c)2, the differential cross section can vary by several orders of magnitude, even for a given target nucleus. This fact, combined with the relatively high cross sections, makes quasielastic scattering an excellent means of studying the Nuclear Medium Modification of hadrons. In this paper, the scaling of the differential cross section with the fourth power of the nuclear mass is shown to be a natural consequence of the eikonal approximation, valid for low inelasticities. This scaling is illustrated in quasielastic scattering from nuclei and is shown to provide a remarkably good agreement with experimental data from a variety of nuclei. The proposed scaling has two important applications. First, it allows for extraction of cross sections for elementary scattering processes from measurements of the average nuclear cross section. Second, it allows for predictions of quasielastic scattering amplitudes from structures inferred from other types of scattering. These applications are illustrated using examples from the field of Neutron Scattering.

Title:
Fifteen Years of High-Resolution Radio Imaging of Supernova 1987A.
Abstract:
human_text:
Supernova 1987A in the Large Magellanic Cloud provides a spectacularly
detailed view of the aftermath of a core-collapse explosion. The supernova
ejecta initially coasted outward at more than 10% of the speed of light, but in
1990 were observed to decelerate rapidly as they began to encounter dense
circumstellar material expelled by the progenitor star. The resulting shock has
subsequently produced steadily brightening radio synchrotron emission, which is
resolved by the Australia Telescope Compact Array (ATCA) into an expanding
limb-brightened shell. Here we present 15 years of ATCA imaging of Supernova
1987A, at an effective angular resolution of 0.4 arcsec. We find that the radio
remnant has accelerated in its expansion over this period, from approx 3600
km/s in 1992 to approx 5200 km/s at the end of 2006. The published diameters of
the evolving X-ray shell have been ~15% smaller than the corresponding radio
values, but a simultaneous Fourier analysis of both radio and X-ray data
eliminates this discrepancy, and yields a current diameter for the shell in
both wave-bands of approx 1.7 arcsec. An asymmetric brightness distribution is
seen in radio images at all ATCA epochs: the eastern and western rims have
higher fluxes than the northern and southern regions, indicating that most of
the radio emission comes from the equatorial plane of the system, where the
progenitor star's circumstellar wind is thought to be densest. The eastern lobe
is brighter than and further from the supernova site than the western lobe,
suggesting an additional asymmetry in the initial distribution of supernova
ejecta.
machine_text: Supernova 1987A was one of the closest and best observed supernova in decades. Fifteen years after the explosion, observations at radio wavelengths still play an important role in our understanding of this object. In this paper, we present high-resolution images of SN 1987A at 14 different radio frequencies between 76 MHz and 14.5 GHz. We use data from the Multibeam Observing System on the Australia Telescope Compact Array, the Jansky Very Large Array, the LOw Frequency ARray, the Robert C. Byrd Green Bank Telescope, and the Pinwheel Radio Telescope to produce the highest-resolution (between 3.4 and 22 AU at different frequencies) and most completely sampled (every two hours for 15 years) images of SN 1987A to date. We discuss our findings in the context of current three-dimensional models of the SN and conclude with a summary of the remarkable legacy of SN 1987A.

Title:
Exact Floquet states of a driven condensate and their stabilities.
Abstract:
human_text:
We investigate the Gross-Pitaevskii equation for a classically chaotic
system, which describes an atomic Bose-Einstein condensate confined in an
optical lattice and driven by a spatiotemporal periodic laser field. It is
demonstrated that the exact Floquet states appear when the external
time-dependent potential is balanced by the nonlinear mean-field interaction.
The balance region of parameters is divided into a phase-continuing region and
a phase-jumping one. In the latter region, the Floquet states are
spatiotemporal vortices of nontrivial phase structures and zero-density cores.
Due to the velocity singularities of vortex cores and the blowing-up of
perturbed solutions, the spatiotemporal vortices are unstable periodic states
embedded in chaos. The stability and instability of these Floquet states are
numerically explored by the time evolution of fidelity between the exact and
numerical solutions. It is numerically illustrated that the stable Floquet
states could be prepared from the uniformly initial states by slow growth of
the external potential.
machine_text: Theoretical studies of dynamical systems provide insights into many physical, chemical and biological processes. An excellent example is the harmonic oscillator which describes the resonant behaviour of a driven system coupled to a linear force. In Bose-Einstein condensate (BEC) atoms subjected to harmonic driving, the problem is mathematically identical but additionally complicated by nonlinear interactions. The Gross-Pitaevskii (GP) equation describes the condensate wave function and it is useful to reduce the problem to that of a nonlinear Schrödinger equation. This is usually done by performing a slowly varying amplitude approximation. The resulting equation, known as the Stuart-Landau equation, is analytically tractable and has been used to describe a diverse range of phenomena, including the existence and stability of exact analytic solutions. We present such exact analytic solutions in the form of spatiotemporal wave packets which, in the absence of disorder, are found to be unstable. By adding harmonic trapping and dissipation terms, we show that the system can be stabilized, and that such wave packets can be made stable via the addition of disorder. This disorder may be realised through a random perturbation to the coefficients of the Stuart-Landau equation. We demonstrate this by calculating the average wave packet properties for many realizations of the disorder. Using this approach, we can engineer the condensate to have wave packet mobility. Finally, we provide a guide to the rich variety of phenomena that can be realised using the GP equation with driving.

Title:
Measurement of Ultra-Low Potassium Contaminations with Accelerator Mass Spectrometry.
Abstract:
human_text:
Levels of trace radiopurity in active detector materials is a subject of
major concern in low-background experiments. Among the radio-isotopes, $\k40$
is one of the most abundant and yet whose signatures are difficult to reject.
Procedures were devised to measure trace potassium concentrations in the
inorganic salt CsI as well as in organic liquid scintillator (LS) with
Accelerator Mass Spectrometry (AMS), giving, respectively, the
$\k40$-contamination levels of $\sim 10^{-10}$ and $\sim 10^{-13}$ g/g.
Measurement flexibilities and sensitivities are improved over conventional
methods. The projected limiting sensitivities if no excess of potassium signals
had been observed over background are $8 \times 10^{-13}$ g/g and $3 \times
10^{-17}$ g/g for the CsI and LS, respectively. Studies of the LS samples
indicate that the radioactive contaminations come mainly in the dye solutes,
while the base solvents are orders of magnitude cleaner. The work demonstrate
the possibilities of measuring naturally-occurring isotopes with the AMS
techniques.
machine_text: Ultra-low level potassium contaminations in atmospheric air (ppb, parts per billion) have serious impacts on human health and strongly limit the capability of air analysis with conventional methods. In this work, a novel approach for potassium measurement based on accelerator mass spectrometry is presented. This technique allows for the determination of potassium at levels as low as 0.5 ppb in air with a precision of better than 1%. The new method allows to overcome the major limitations of conventional techniques and to provide improved knowledge of potassium contamination in the atmosphere. The demonstrated capabilities allow for the detection of ultra-low potassium levels in several industrial environments and urban canyons. Applications for the evaluation of potassium air pollution and human health risk assessment are presented. The measurement of atmospheric potassium at levels lower than 0.1 ppm has been demonstrated in the past using sophisticated devices based on atomic absorption spectrometry. This work reports a significant improvement in the technique sensitivity enabling the measurement of potassium at levels as low as 0.5 ppb (part per billion). The key feature of the method is the use of a low background radioactive source to monitor the entire sample analysis. This allows potassium determination with a precision better than 1% even for potassium levels as low as 50 ppb. The new approach was validated using measurements of atmospheric potassium in several industrial environments and urban canyons. The demonstrated capabilities allow for the detection of ultra-low potassium levels in the atmosphere, down to the level of 0.5 ppb. The new method allows for the evaluation of potassium air pollution and human health risk assessment.

Title:
Double solid twistor spaces: the case of arbitrary signature.
Abstract:
human_text:
In a recent paper (math.DG/0701278) we constructed a series of new Moishezon
twistor spaces which is a kind of variant of the famous LeBrun twistor spaces.
In this paper we explicitly give projective models of another series of
Moishezon twistor spaces on nCP^2 for arbitrary n>2, which can be regarded as a
generalization of the twistor spaces of a 'double solid type' on 3CP^2 studied
by Kreussler, Kurke, Poon and the author. Similarly to the twistor spaces of
'double solid type' on 3CP^2, projective models of present twistor spaces have
a natural structure of double covering of a CP^2-bundle over CP^1. We
explicitly give a defining polynomial of the branch divisor of the double
covering whose restriction to fibers are degree four. If n>3 these are new
twistor spaces, to the best of the author's knowledge. We also compute the
dimension of the moduli space of these twistor spaces. Differently from
math.DG/0701278, the present investigation is based on analysis of
pluri-(half-)anticanonical systems of the twistor spaces.
machine_text: In eighties, Hitchin introduced a twistor space for every signature (4p, 0, s), generalizing the usual cases p = 0, +4 and s = 0, -4. In this paper we study the family of double solid twistor spaces, corresponding to the signature (4, 0, 0). We provide a new simple description in terms of finite flat groupoids, which has the advantage to work for arbitrary genus. This article is a transcription of a paper submitted to the arXiv on May 10, 2020. It remains available there for 15 days and then, by acceptance, it will become available in the www archive of the author's institution. Introduction. The Hitchin's double solid twistor space is the twistor space over the signature (4, 0, 0). It was introduced in the eighties by Hitchin [1], generalizing the usual cases p = 0, +4 and s = 0, -4. Let Ω be the vector bundle of the octonions, with the quadratic form defined by the intersection with the imaginary four-sphere. Ω is a positive line bundle over 8-dim quadric surface Q. The twistor space is defined by the orthogonal split of the twistor space Χ(Q) over Q, whose fiber is the Stiefel manifold of Ω-spinors. Such an orthogonal splitting allows to identify the total space of Ω with the projectivized spin bundle of Q, where the projectivized spinor bundle is defined as the quotient of the bundle of two-forms by the complexification of the orthogonal of Ω. We provide a new simple description in terms of finite flat groupoids. This description has the advantage to work for arbitrary genus. Finite flat groupoids were introduced by Kobayashi andNomizu [7]. Finally, we discuss the conformal and projective structures on a double solid. * Groupoids. Finite flat groupoids were introduced by Kobayashi and Nomizu [7]. Let G be a Lie groupoid over M, where M is a smooth manifold. Such a structure is given by the following data: 1) an orthogonal structure on the tangent bundle TM of G; 2) an action of G on its unit space Υ(G) such that the differential restricts to an action on the soul Υ(M) of G; 3) an injective morphism of groupoids from G to the projectivized frame bundle of the orthogonal structure on TM; the structure of groupoid on G induces an injective morphism from G to the projectivized spin bundle of Υ(G). An example of finite flat groupoid is the structure of Lie groupoid on the orthogonal frame bundle of a Riemannian manifold. Another example is the automorphism groupoid of a Lie group, considered as a groupoid structure on the left cosets of the group.
