Title:
Socioeconomic Networks with Long-Range Interactions.
Abstract:
human_text:
We study a modified version of a model previously proposed by Jackson and
Wolinsky to account for communicating information and allocating goods in
socioeconomic networks. In the model, the utility function of each node is
given by a weighted sum of contributions from all accessible nodes. The
weights, parameterized by the variable $\delta$, decrease with distance. We
introduce a growth mechanism where new nodes attach to the existing network
preferentially by utility. By increasing $\delta$, the network structure
evolves from a power-law to an exponential degree distribution, passing through
a regime characterised by shorter average path length, lower degree
assortativity and higher central point dominance. In the second part of the
paper we compare different network structures in terms of the average utility
received by each node. We show that power-law networks provide higher average
utility than Poisson random networks. This provides a possible justification
for the ubiquitousness of scale-free networks in the real world.
machine_text: Networks have been a powerful tool to analyze relationships between entities, and uncovering structures behind networks have led to remarkable advances in many disciplines, including physics, biology, social sciences, and computer sciences. The most common types of networks areUndirected networks where the connections between any two nodes does not depend on whether other nodes are connected to the first two nodes. Most social and economic networks are undirected, and the vast majority of theoretical network studies have been based on undirected networks. Weighted networks and directed networks where the direction of connections is used to encode directional information are also popular, and have provided significant new insights.In this paper, I introduce a novel network construction technique based on a class of nonlinear models with long-range interactions. A network structure is encoded into the model by considering a generic function of pairwise distances between nodes, and the model is fitted to data via maximum likelihood. Unlike existing network models that often involve intractable integrals or computationally prohibitive Markov chain Monte Carlo algorithms, my method is based on fast Fourier transform that allows for likelihood computations in polynomial time in the number of nodes. The approach is validated on a number of synthetic and real networks, and shown to provide significantly better fits than existing techniques.

Title:
Matching WMAP 3-yrs results with the Cosmological Slingshot Primordial Spectrum.
Abstract:
human_text:
We consider a recently proposed scenario for the generation of primordial
cosmological perturbations, the so called Cosmological Slingshot scenario. We
firstly obtain a general expression for the Slingshot primordial power spectrum
which extends previous results by including a blue pre-bounce residual
contribution at large scales. Starting from this expression we numerically
compute the CMB temperature and polarization power spectra arising from the
Slingshot scenario and show that they excellently match the standard WMAP
3-years best-fit results. In particular, if the residual blue spectrum is far
above the largest WMAP observed scale, the Slingshot primordial spectrum fits
the data well by only fixing its amplitude and spectral index at the pivot
scale k_p=10^{-3}h x Mpc^{-1}. We finally show that all possible distinctive
Slingshot signatures in the CMB power spectra are confined to very low
multipoles and thus very hard to detect due to large cosmic variance dominated
error bars at these scales.
machine_text: Theoretical physicists have recently proposed a new paradigm, called the Slingshot mechanism, to explain the success of the inflationary paradigm. In this model, our universe popped into existence near a boundary of another, larger universe. This boundary has a highly curved geometry, which could lead to fluctuation of the metric across the boundary. These metric fluctuations can act as a stochastic gravitational wave background (SWB), which seeds the formation of structures in the universe. We calculate the power spectrum of SWB generated in the Slingshot model, and compare it with the power spectrum of Primordial scalar spectrum (PS) calculated by the WMAP team. We show that, for some parameter choices, the SWB and PS are nearly identical. We conclude that a concrete realization of the Slingshot model could account for the success of inflation without the need for fine-tuning. The full paper is available here: https://arxiv.org/pdf/2004.11164.pdf

Title:
Improved constraints on dark energy from Chandra X-ray observations of the largest relaxed galaxy clusters.
Abstract:
human_text:
We present constraints on the mean matter density, Omega_m, dark energy
density, Omega_de, and the dark energy equation of state parameter, w, using
Chandra measurements of the X-ray gas mass fraction (fgas) in 42 hot (kT>5keV),
X-ray luminous, dynamically relaxed galaxy clusters spanning the redshift range
0.05<z<1.1. Using only the fgas data for the 6 lowest redshift clusters at
z<0.15, for which dark energy has a negligible effect on the measurements, we
measure Omega_m=0.28+-0.06 (68% confidence, using standard priors on the Hubble
Constant, H_0, and mean baryon density, Omega_bh^2). Analyzing the data for all
42 clusters, employing only weak priors on H_0 and Omega_bh^2, we obtain a
similar result on Omega_m and detect the effects of dark energy on the
distances to the clusters at ~99.99% confidence, with Omega_de=0.86+-0.21 for a
non-flat LCDM model. The detection of dark energy is comparable in significance
to recent SNIa studies and represents strong, independent evidence for cosmic
acceleration. Systematic scatter remains undetected in the fgas data, despite a
weighted mean statistical scatter in the distance measurements of only ~5%. For
a flat cosmology with constant w, we measure Omega_m=0.28+-0.06 and
w=-1.14+-0.31. Combining the fgas data with independent constraints from CMB
and SNIa studies removes the need for priors on Omega_bh^2 and H_0 and leads to
tighter constraints: Omega_m=0.253+-0.021 and w=-0.98+-0.07 for the same
constant-w model. More general analyses in which we relax the assumption of
flatness and/or allow evolution in w remain consistent with the cosmological
constant paradigm. Our analysis includes conservative allowances for systematic
uncertainties. The small systematic scatter and tight constraints bode well for
future dark energy studies using the fgas method. (Abridged)
machine_text: The dark energy, which is interpreted as a component of the universe with negative pressure, is one of the biggest mysteries in modern physics. One of the most promising ways of measuring its properties is based on the distance based cosmology called ‘Cosmic Distance duality relations’ (DDGR), which connect the angular diameter distance to the last scattering surface, dA, with the luminosity distance, dL, to the observed galaxy cluster. So far, these relations have been tested only on small cluster samples (e.g. Sunyaev-Zeldovich (SZ) effect, gravitational lensing) and with low accuracy (mainly due to the poor calibration of the local distance ladder). I present the results of X-ray observations of the largest, most relaxed galaxy clusters with the Chandra X-ray observatory. These clusters follow the cosmic distance duality relation to an accuracy of ~8%, which is an improvement of a factor of 5 compared to earlier results. The derived precise X-ray masses, which are used to test the cosmological models, are also presented.

Title:
Universality of Mixed Action Extrapolation Formulae.
Abstract:
human_text:
Mixed action theories with chirally symmetric valence fermions exhibit very
desirable features both at the level of the lattice calculations as well as in
the construction and implementation of the low energy mixed action effective
field theory. In this work we show that when such a mixed action effective
field theory is projected onto the valence sector, both the Lagrangian and the
extrapolation formulae become universal in form through next to leading order,
for all variants of discretization methods used for the sea fermions. Our
conclusion relies on the chiral nature of the valence quarks. The result
implies that for all sea quark methods which are in the same universality class
as QCD, the numerical values of the physical coefficients in the various mixed
action chiral Lagrangians will be the same up to lattice spacing dependent
corrections. This allows us to construct a prescription to determine the mixed
action extrapolation formulae for a large class of hadronic correlation
functions computed in partially quenched chiral perturbation theory at the
one-loop level. For specific examples, we apply this prescription to the
nucleon twist--2 matrix elements and the nucleon--nucleon system. In addition,
we determine the mixed action extrapolation formula for the neutron EDM as this
provides a nice example of a theta-dependent observable; these observables are
exceptions to our prescription.
machine_text: The universality of Mixed Action Extrapolation (MEA) formulae, which link free energies of lattice models to the covering radius of the lattice, is demonstrated by explicit calculations of the five- and six-state Potts models in two and three dimensions. For the first time MEA is shown to be exact in the thermodynamic limit, both in the two- and three-dimensional Potts models. This is done using a combination of analytical and numerical techniques. The universality of MEA formulae implies that, for any given lattice and lattice models, the free energy difference between two arbitrary boundary conditions separated by a distance R in the thermodynamic limit can be written in the form \[ \Delta F(R) \approx f(R/L) \sim \ln R/L + \cdots \text{, as } R \to \infty, \] where L is the lattice size and R is the covering radius of the lattice. The covering radius is a geometric property of the lattice and has a simple expression in terms of the interaction parameters of the lattice models.

Title:
A twisted FZZ-like dual for the two-dimensional black hole.
Abstract:
human_text:
We review and study the duality between string theory formulated on a curved
exact background (the two dimensional black hole) and string theory in flat
space with a tachyon-like potential. We generalize previous results in this
subject by discussing a twisted version of the
Fateev-Zamolodchikov-Zamolodchikov conjecture. This duality is shown to hold at
the level of N-point correlation functions on the sphere topology, and connects
tree-level string amplitudes in the Euclidean version of the 2D black hole (x
time) to correlation functions in a non-linear sigma-model in flat space but in
presence of a tachyon wall potential and a linear dilaton. The dual CFT
corresponds to the perturbed 2D quantum gravity coupled to c<1 matter (x time),
where the operator that describes the tachyon-like potential can be seen as a
n=2 momentum mode perturbation, while the usual sine-Liouville operator would
correspond to the vortex sector n =1. We show how the sine-Liouville
interaction term arises through a twisting of the marginal deformation
introduced here, and discuss such 'twisting' as a non-trivial realization of
the symmetries of the theory. After briefly reviewing the computation of
correlation functions in sine-Liouville CFT, we give a precise prescription for
computing correlation functions in the twisted model. To show the new version
of the correspondence we make use of a formula recently proven by S. Ribault
and J. Teschner, which connects the correlation functions in the
Wess-Zumino-Witten theory to correlation functions in the Liouville theory.
Conversely, the duality discussed here can be thought of as a free field
realization of such remarkable formula.

The R-R sector of the theory contains the space-time bosons and fermions as well as the corresponding solitonic states. This model can be obtained from the usual FZZ T-duality transformation applied to the reversed NS-NS sector of the Type IIA superstring theory with O8-planes, with the O8-planes representing the twisted R-R sector. As an application, we study this theory in the low-energy limit and demonstrate that it is a consistent truncation of the four-dimensional $N=4$ super-Yang-Mills theory coupled to matter hypermultiplets in the quiver gauge group, with the R-R bosons corresponding to the vector superfield of the low-energy effective theory. We also demonstrate that the low-energy limit of this superstring theory possesses the $SL(2,\mathbb{R})/U(1)$ global symmetry, which is the same as the global symmetry of the four-dimensional effective super Yang-Mills theory with respect to the $N=2$ supersymmetry.

Title:
Conserved spin Hall conductance in two dimensional electron gas in a perpendicular magnetic field.
Abstract:
human_text:
Using the microscopic theory of the conserved spin current [Phys. Rev. Lett.
\textbf{96}, 076604 (2006)], we investigate the spin Hall effect in the two
dimensional electron gas system with a perpendicular magnetic field. The spin
Hall conductance $\sigma_{\mu\nu}^{s}$ as a response to the electric field
consists of two parts, i.e., the conventional part $\sigma_{\mu\nu}^{s0}$ and
the spin torque dipole correction $\sigma_{\mu\nu}^{s\tau}$. It is shown that
the spin-orbit coupling competes with Zeeman splitting by introducing
additional degeneracies between different Landau levels at certain values of
magnetic field. These degeneracies, if occurring at the Fermi level, turn to
give rise to resonances in both $\sigma_{\mu\nu}^{s0}$ and $\sigma_{\mu\nu
}^{s\tau}$ in spin Hall conductance. Remarkably, both of these two components
have the same sign in the wide range of variation in the magnetic field, which
result in an overall enhancement of the total spin Hall current. In particular,
the magnitude of $\sigma_{\mu\nu}^{s\tau}$ is much larger than that of
$\sigma_{\mu\nu}^{s0}$ around the resonance.
machine_text: In two dimensional electron gas (2DEG) with spin-orbit coupling, a conserved spin Hall conductance can exist in the absence of a net spin polarization. In this work, we report that the spin Hall conductance is still conserved even when a net spin polarization does exist. We show that the spin Hall conductance is related to the Berry curvature of the dressed electronic states and is therefore time-reversal invariant. The conserved spin Hall conductance is then shown to lead to a dissipationless charge spin current even in the presence of a nonzero magnetization current. We calculate this spin current within a self-consistent Born approximation and find that it is linear in the magnetization current, in agreement with the Kubo formula for the spin Hall conductivity. Finally, we discuss experimental implications of our results. We construct a low energy effective theory for the 2DEG with Rashba spin-orbit coupling in a perpendicular magnetic field. By performing a functional derivative, we derive the effective action in terms of fermions with four-component spinor notation. By making a Schrieffer-Wolff transformation and linearizing the dispersion around the Dirac points, we obtain the low energy effective Hamiltonian. It contains four pair of Weyl fermions with opposite chirality. The pairing between the Weyl fermions with opposite chiralities is controlled by the inter-valley (spin) coupling, which is generated by a quantum correction to the gauge field. This spin coupling term is odd under time-reversal and enforces a conserved spin Hall conductance in the system. We then consider a setup with an applied electric field in the direction transverse to the 2DEG plane and spin-dependent magnetic fields in the plane. In the presence of these, there will be a charge and spin current. While the charge current is accompanied by a voltage drop in the magnetic leads, the spin current is not. It is instead associated with a dissipationless transverse spin magnetization, which is independent of the voltage applied to the leads. The origin of the dissipationless transverse spin magnetization is the spin coupling term generated by the quantum corrections to the gauge field, which enforces a conserved spin Hall conductance in the system.

Title:
A Bayesian approach to strong lensing modelling of galaxy clusters.
Abstract:
human_text:
In this paper, we describe a procedure for modelling strong lensing galaxy
clusters with parametric methods, and to rank models quantitatively using the
Bayesian evidence. We use a publicly available Markov chain Monte-Carlo (MCMC)
sampler ('Bayesys'), allowing us to avoid local minima in the likelihood
functions. To illustrate the power of the MCMC technique, we simulate three
clusters of galaxies, each composed of a cluster-scale halo and a set of
perturbing galaxy-scale subhalos. We ray-trace three light beams through each
model to produce a catalogue of multiple images, and then use the MCMC sampler
to recover the model parameters in the three different lensing configurations.
We find that, for typical Hubble Space Telescope (HST)-quality imaging data,
the total mass in the Einstein radius is recovered with ~1-5% error according
to the considered lensing configuration. However, we find that the mass of the
galaxies is strongly degenerated with the cluster mass when no multiple images
appear in the cluster centre. The mass of the galaxies is generally recovered
with a 20% error, largely due to the poorly constrained cut-off radius.
Finally, we describe how to rank models quantitatively using the Bayesian
evidence. We confirm the ability of strong lensing to constrain the mass
profile in the central region of galaxy clusters in this way. Ultimately, such
a method applied to strong lensing clusters with a very large number of
multiple images may provide unique geometrical constraints on cosmology. The
implementation of the MCMC sampler used in this paper has been done within the
framework of the Lenstool software package, which is publicly available.
machine_text: Strong lensing, also called gravitational lensing, is the phenomenon by which light from a distant background galaxy is bent due to the Gravitational field of cluster galaxies. It is one of the most powerful methods to study the dark matter distribution in clusters of galaxies. Bayesian inference provides a powerful framework to extract the maximum information from the raw imaging data, while appropriately handling missing or erroneous data points. I present a Bayesian Markov Chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) algorithm to model the cluster mass distribution, combining strong and weak lensing data. I demonstrate the effectiveness of the algorithm on both simulated and real data using statistical tools to diagnose the convergence of the MCMC chains. The method presented in this paper can be extended to study other astrophysical problems which can be modeled with MCMC methods. This work was performed under the auspices of the European Union’s Framework Programme for Research and Innovation (2014-2020) under the aegis of the Marie Skłodowska-Curie Research Training Network GA Edge Networks (GA 662765).

Title:

human_text:
The observation of neutrino oscillations requires new physics beyond the
standard model (SM). A SM-like gauge theory with p lepton families can be
extended by introducing q heavy right-handed Majorana neutrinos but preserving
its SU(2)_L x U(1)_Y gauge symmetry. The overall neutrino mass matrix M turns
out to be a symmetric (p+q) x (p+q) matrix. Given p>q, the rank of M is in
general equal to 2q, corresponding to 2q non-zero mass eigenvalues. The
existence of (p-q) massless left-handed Majorana neutrinos is an exact
consequence of the model, independent of the usual approximation made in
deriving the Type-I seesaw relation between the effective p x p light Majorana
neutrino mass matrix M_\nu and the q x q heavy Majorana neutrino mass matrix
M_R. In other words, the numbers of massive left- and right-handed neutrinos
are fairly matched. A good example to illustrate this seesaw fair play rule is
the minimal seesaw model with p=3 and q=2, in which one massless neutrino sits
on the unbalanced seesaw.

We find an upper bound on their masses for a given value of the lightest neutrino mass. Title:
On Cuspidal Representations of General Linear Groups over Discrete Valuation Rings.
Abstract:
human_text:
We define a new notion of cuspidality for representations of $\GL_n$ over a
finite quotient $\Oh_k$ of the ring of integers $\Oh$ of a non-Archimedean
local field $F$ using geometric and infinitesimal induction functors, which
involve automorphism groups $G_\lambda$ of torsion $\Oh$\nobreakdash-modules.
When $n$ is a prime, we show that this notion of cuspidality is equivalent to
strong cuspidality, which arises in the construction of supercuspidal
representations of $\GL_n(F)$. We show that strongly cuspidal representations
share many features of cuspidal representations of finite general linear
groups. In the function field case, we show that the construction of the
representations of $\GL_n(\Oh_k)$ for $k\geq 2$ for all $n$ is equivalent to
the construction of the representations of all the groups $G_\lambda$. A
functional equation for zeta functions for representations of $\GL_n(\Oh_k)$ is
established for representations which are not contained in an infinitesimally
induced representation. All the cuspidal representations for $\GL_4(\Oh_2)$ are
constructed. Not all these representations are strongly cuspidal.
machine_text: Representations of general linear groups over discrete valuation rings (DVRs) were extensively studied. Over a decade ago, Schneider and Teitelbaum constructed such representations via adèlic locally analytic vectors. Since then, many new constructions have been given using narrow frames, local orbits, and seminorms on representations. Each of these new constructions provided additional insight into the problem of constructing irreducible cuspidal representations. In this paper, we give a unifying construction, which applies to any DVR with perfect residue field and fraction field of characteristic zero, and yields irreducible cuspidal representations. Our construction is direct, and provides many additional examples of irreducible cuspidal representations that were not previously known. Finally, we show that our construction interpolates between the existing constructions. This work was performed while the author was in residence at the American Institute of Mathematics in Palo Alto, CA, during the spring 2017 semester.

Title:
Pair Correlation Functions and a Free-Energy Functional for the Nematic Phase.
Abstract:
human_text:
In this paper we have presented the calculation of pair correlation functions
in a nematic phase for a model of spherical particles with the long-range
anisotropic interaction from the mean spherical approximation(MSA) and the
Percus-Yevick (PY) integral equation theories. The results found from the MSA
theory have been compared with those found analytically by Holovko and
Sokolovska (J. Mol. Liq. $\bf 82$, 161(1999)). A free energy functional which
involves both the symmetry conserving and symmetry broken parts of the direct
pair correlation function has been used to study the properties of the nematic
phase. We have also examined the possibility of constructing a free energy
functional with the direct pair correlation function which includes only the
principal order parameter of the ordered phase and found that the resulting
functional gives results that are in good agreement with the original
functional. The isotropic-nematic transition has been located using the grand
thermodynamic potential. The PY theory has been found to give nematic phase
with pair correlation function harmonic coefficients having all the desired
features. In a nematic phase the harmonic coefficient of the total pair
correlation function $h({\bf x_1},{\bf x_2})$ connected with the correlations
of the director transverse fluctuations should develop a long-range tail. This
feature has been found in both the MSA and PY theories.
machine_text: Nematic liquid crystals are partially ordered phases with rod-like molecules aligned along a particular axis. In the bulk, the alignment direction is usually constant for all positions, but at the surface the molecules may be freely orientated. This leads to an enrichment of nematic order at the surfaces, which is commonly referred to as surface nematic order. Here we present a simple Landau-de Gennes description of a surface nematic liquid crystal, focussing on the case where the surface enrichment is weak. In our approach, the director is described by a continuous variable θ(z, x), where z is the normal direction to the surface and x is the lateral spatial variable. The order parameter adopts a constant value s in the surface layer, leading to a surface free energy functional which can be minimized with respect to s and θ. By applying different asymptotic approximations we are able to characterize the isotropic, N- and Sm-Nematic phases and the corresponding phase transitions. To quantify the degree of order, we introduce pair correlation functions g12(x) and g22(x), which for a Nematic phase take on a non-zero constant value. The values of g12 and g22 depend on the spatial correlation of the order parameter, and can be determined by solving an approximate anisotropic Laplace equation. From the functional we are able to derive a Cahn-Hilliard equation for the order parameter evolution, which can be simplified to a linear non-local diffusion equation by performing a gradient expansion. This diffusion equation can be solved using an appropriate random initial condition to give the order parameter distribution at long times, and from this we are able to extract the values of g12 and g22 at long distances. As an application, we discuss the case of a surface enrichment which varies quadratically with z, and which leads to modified power-law decay of g12 and g22. Finally, we also present the corresponding results for the special case of a step function surface enrichment.

Title:

Abstract:
human_text:
Far-infrared (IR) images of the nearby Sb galaxy NGC2841 and the Sc galaxy
NGC2976 at wavelengths of 65, 90, 140, and 160 um have been obtained with the
Far-Infrared Surveyor (FIS) onboard AKARI. Both galaxies reveal similar
morphologies of dust rings. They are, however, significantly different in the
dust temperature: a cold (21 K) ring for NGC2841 and a warm (30 K) ring for

structure for the different Hubble type of the galaxy. In addition to the dust
ring structure, a warm dust component is detected from the central region of

Emission-line Region nucleus. As for NGC2976, an extended dust component is
observed along the minor axis, which shows a distribution somewhat asymmetrical
to the galactic disk; this might be associated with the HI bridge in the
M81/M82 group that NGC2976 belongs to. By taking advantage of a wealth of the

distribution of NGC2841 is spatially more variable than that of NGC2976.

Title:

Abstract:

telescope with silicon carbide mirrors. The wavefront error of the AKARI
telescope obtained in laboratory measurements at 9 K showed that expected
in-orbit imaging performance was diffraction-limited at a wavelength of 6.2 um.

Title:
The early evolution of tidal dwarf galaxies.
Abstract:
human_text:
Context: Dwarf galaxies can arise from self-gravitating structures emerging
from tidal tails. What fraction of the known dwarf galaxies in the Local
Universe can have this origin is still a matter of debate. Aims: In our effort
to understand the origin and evolution of tidal dwarf galaxies and their
correspondence with local objects, the first step is to understand how these
galaxies (which are supposed to have a limited amount of dark matter) react to
the feedback of the ongoing star formation. Methods: We make use of 2-D
chemodynamical calculations in order to study the early evolution of isolated,
dark matter-free dwarf galaxies. We present models in which feedback parameters
are varied. We also compare the results with dark matter-dominated dwarf galaxy
models. Results: All the considered models show that the star formation
proceeds for more than 300 Myr, therefore dwarf galaxies without large dark
matter halos are not necessarily quickly destroyed. The chemical evolution of
these objects is consistent with the main chemical properties of the dSphs of
the Local Group. Models with large dark matter halos show results consistent
with models free of dark matter, indicating that the distribution of gas is
more important than the depth of the potential well in determining the global
behaviour of dSph-sized dwarf galaxies.

They may form in response to high-speed collisions between dwarf galaxies, and as such, are excellent probes of hierarchical structure formation. Their properties can be predicted by a simple empirical law, and they are used as tools to study the processes of galaxy formation and evolution. In this work, we compile a database of TDGs from the literature, with a total of 77 TDGs in 21 Hickson Compact Groups (HCGs). We present detailed models of the photometric evolution of these systems, and compare the predictions of these models to available data for 53 systems. We find that (1) the most massive TDGs in HCGs must have acquired more than 90% of their current mass by less than 8.5 Gyr, with most acquiring more than 50% of their current mass by less than 6 Gyr; (2) low surface brightness TDGs are predicted to have masses of 0.1-1.0%, with a median of 0.3% of the total group mass; (3) the characteristic mass scale for TDGs scales with the total mass of the HCG; and (4) there is no strong correlation between the age of a TDG and its mass, color, or environment. This suggests that tidal stripping and merging have been important processes in shaping the TDG population in HCGs. We conclude by discussing the implications of these results for hierarchical structure formation and the evolution of low surface brightness galaxies.

Title:

Abstract:

The paper presents results from a small survey of 22 young, nearby stars that
was designed to detect substellar companions and ultimately giant extrasolar
planets down to Jupiter masses. The targets are members of the Tucana and Beta
Pictoris moving groups apart from the somewhat older star HIP 71395 that has a
radial velocity trend suggesting a massive planet in large orbit. The survey
was carried out in the L-band using adaptive optics assisted imaging with
NAOS-CONICA (NACO) at the VLT. The chosen observation wavelength is well suited
to search for close companions around young stars and delivers unprecedented
detection limits. The presented technique reaches some of the best
sensitivities as of today and is currently the most sensitive method for the
contrast limited detection of substellar companions that are cooler than about
1000K. The companion to 51 Eri, GJ 3305, was found to be a very close binary on
an eccentric orbit. No substellar companions were found around the target
stars, although the method permitted to detect companions down to a few Jupiter
masses at orbital distances of typically 5 astronomical units. A planet with a
mass >1 M_Jup at distances >5 AU around AU Mic can be excluded at the time of
our observations. The absence of detected planets sets constraints on the
frequency distribution and maximum orbital distance of giant exoplanets. For
example, a radial distribution power law index of 0.2 in combination with a
maximum orbital radius exceeding 30 AU can be rejected at a 90% confidence
level.

This work presents the first direct detection of infrared radiation from the region around giant planets in the habitable zones of nearby stars. This is done using L-band (3.78-3.84 μm) spectroscopy, which has not been widely used for planet detection because it is more difficult to observe from space than other bands, and does not provide the same level of detail as shorter wavelengths. Using the Infrared Telescope on board the Spitzer Space Observatory, we obtained high-quality spectroscopy of two nearby stars, named Tucana and Beta Pictoris, that are members of the moving groups corresponding to their age. We observed each star in the L' (3.74-3.81 μm) and L" (3.84-3.94 μm) water vapor filters, which are extremely sensitive to reflected infrared radiation from planets in the habitable zone of these stars. Title:
Many concepts and two logics of algorithmic reduction.
Abstract:
human_text:
Within the program of finding axiomatizations for various parts of
computability logic, it was proved earlier that the logic of interactive Turing
reduction is exactly the implicative fragment of Heyting's intuitionistic
calculus. That sort of reduction permits unlimited reusage of the computational
resource represented by the antecedent. An at least equally basic and natural
sort of algorithmic reduction, however, is the one that does not allow such
reusage. The present article shows that turning the logic of the first sort of
reduction into the logic of the second sort of reduction takes nothing more
than just deleting the contraction rule from its Gentzen-style axiomatization.
The first (Turing) sort of interactive reduction is also shown to come in three
natural versions. While those three versions are very different from each
other, their logical behaviors (in isolation) turn out to be indistinguishable,
with that common behavior being precisely captured by implicative
intuitionistic logic. Among the other contributions of the present article is
an informal introduction of a series of new -- finite and bounded -- versions
of recurrence operations and the associated reduction operations. An online
source on computability logic can be found at
http://www.cis.upenn.edu/~giorgi/cl.html
machine_text: Algorithmic reduction is a fundamental and challenging problem. By now, two distinct but related logics of algorithmic reduction have been developed and explored. One focuses on computational complexity, and is based on relativization. The other focuses on language shift, and is based on Rewrite Rule Semantics (RRS). This work unifies these two logics by introducing a novel intermediate level called behavioral equivalence, and develops a framework to capture both computational and language shift aspects of algorithmic reduction in a unified way. As a by-product, this framework greatly simplifies and systematizes the previous work on both relativization and RRS. We illustrate the usefulness of our framework by applying it to a series of long-standing open problems, including Champarna’s open problem on the limits of nonuniform samplings, and finally settling it for any $n$, any samplings allowed. Moreover, we propose parameterized solutions to two-sidedif and three-sided pathfinders, and show their equivalence to a well-known open problem on related classes of pushdown systems. We also show that a seemingly different problem called testing emptiness of L systems, which has been a major open problem for more than three decades, is captured by our framework as well.

Title:
Strongly modulated transmission of a spin-split quantum wire with local Rashba interaction.
Abstract:
human_text:
We investigate the transport properties of ballistic quantum wires in the
presence of Zeeman spin splittings and a spatially inhomogeneous Rashba
interaction. The Zeeman interaction is extended along the wire and produces
gaps in the energy spectrum which allow electron propagation only for spinors
lying along a certain direction. For spins in the opposite direction the waves
are evanescent far away from the Rashba region, which plays the role of the
scattering center. The most interesting case occurs when the magnetic field is
perpendicular to the Rashba field. Then, the spins of the asymptotic
wavefunctions are not eigenfunctions of the Rashba Hamiltonian and the
resulting coupling between spins in the Rashba region gives rise to sudden
changes of the transmission probability when the Fermi energy is swept along
the gap. After briefly examining the energy spectrum and eigenfunctions of a
wire with extended Rashba coupling, we analyze the transmission through a
region of localized Rashba interaction, in which a double interface separates a
region of constant Rashba interaction from wire leads free from spin-orbit
coupling. For energies slightly above the propagation threshold, we find the
ubiquitous occurrence of transmission zeros (antiresonances) which are analyzed
by matching methods in the one-dimensional limit. We find that a a minimal
tight-binding model yields analytical transmission lineshapes of Fano
antiresonance type. More general angular dependences of the external magnetic
field is treated within projected Schroedinger equations with Hamiltonian
matrix elements mixing wavefunction components. Finally, we consider a
realistic quantum wire where the energy subbands are coupled via the Rashba
intersubband coupling term and discuss its effect on the transmission zeros.

By using non-equilibrium Green's function method, we find that the transmitted spin-flipped electron spin current is strongly modulated by the wave vector of the electron spin precession in the Rashba interaction region. Due to the destructive interference between the spin-up and spin-down transmission amplitudes, the total spin current becomes nearly zero. However, we also show that the Fano factor, defined as the ratio of the zero-current noise to the mean current, is not suppressed even for strong modulation. In contrast, the zero-frequency noise, which is an indicator of the long-range correlations between the transmitted particles, remains finite even in the deep subband limit. Our results reveal the different roles of the real and momentum scattering in the spin transport of a spin-split quantum wire with Rashba interaction. In order to improve the phasing of the comparable-mass waveform as we
approach the last stable orbit for a system, various re-summation methods have
been used to improve the standard post-Newtonian waveforms. In this work we
present a new family of templates for the detection of gravitational waves from
the inspiral of two comparable-mass black hole binaries. These new adiabatic
templates are based on re-expressing the derivative of the binding energy and
the gravitational wave flux functions in terms of shifted Chebyshev
polynomials. The Chebyshev polynomials are a useful tool in numerical methods
as they display the fastest convergence of any of the orthogonal polynomials.
In this case they are also particularly useful as they eliminate one of the
features that plagues the post-Newtonian expansion. The Chebyshev binding
energy now has information at all post-Newtonian orders, compared to the
post-Newtonian templates which only have information at full integer orders. In
this work, we compare both the post-Newtonian and Chebyshev templates against a

post-Newtonian expansions for the binding energy and flux functions. Our
results show that the Chebyshev templates achieve extremely high fitting
factors at all PN orders and provide excellent parameter extraction. We also
show that this new template family has a faster Cauchy convergence, gives a
better prediction of the position of the Last Stable Orbit and in general
recovers higher Signal-to-Noise ratios than the post-Newtonian templates.

Title:
Magnification relations for Kerr lensing and testing Cosmic Censorship.
Abstract:
human_text:
A Kerr black hole with mass parameter m and angular momentum parameter a
acting as a gravitational lens gives rise to two images in the weak field
limit. We study the corresponding magnification relations, namely the signed
and absolute magnification sums and the centroid up to post-Newtonian order. We
show that there are post-Newtonian corrections to the total absolute
magnification and centroid proportional to a/m, which is in contrast to the
spherically symmetric case where such corrections vanish. Hence we also propose
a new set of lensing observables for the two images involving these
corrections, which should allow measuring a/m with gravitational lensing. In
fact, the resolution capabilities needed to observe this for the Galactic black
hole should in principle be accessible to current and near-future
instrumentation. Since a/m >1 indicates a naked singularity, a most interesting
application would be a test of the Cosmic Censorship conjecture. The technique
used to derive the image properties is based on the degeneracy of the Kerr lens
and a suitably displaced Schwarzschild lens at post-Newtonian order. A simple
physical explanation for this degeneracy is also given.

The photon sphere is an area of spacetime degenerate in gravitational field strength, where gravitational lensing effects are strongest. As a consequence, light is unable to pass through this area from outside the black hole, producing a central bright ring, or “Caustic,” when it passes nearby. In this paper, we study the lensing properties of Kerr black holes with the goal of better understanding how strong-field lensing relates to cosmic censorship, the belief that events across the Universe are well-posed and can be described by classical gravity. In particular, we are interested in relating the position of the Caustic, which is a function of black hole spin and other parameters, to the threshold for classical behavior. We find that the Caustic lies outside the photon sphere for non-extremal Kerr black holes, and that as the spin of the black hole increases, the radius of the photon sphere decreases. Furthermore, we show that when the angular momentum of the black hole is sufficiently high, the size of the Caustic becomes comparable to that of the event horizon. This indicates that strong-field lensing can probe the threshold for classical behavior, and therefore can serve as a test of cosmic censorship.

Title:
The largest eigenvalues of finite rank deformation of large Wigner matrices: convergence and nonuniversality of the fluctuations.
Abstract:
human_text:
In this paper, we investigate the asymptotic spectrum of complex or real
Deformed Wigner matrices $(M_N)_N$ defined by $M_N=W_N/\sqrt{N}+A_N$ where
$W_N$ is an $N\times N$ Hermitian (resp., symmetric) Wigner matrix whose
entries have a symmetric law satisfying a Poincar\'{e} inequality. The matrix
$A_N$ is Hermitian (resp., symmetric) and deterministic with all but finitely
many eigenvalues equal to zero. We first show that, as soon as the first
largest or last smallest eigenvalues of $A_N$ are sufficiently far from zero,
the corresponding eigenvalues of $M_N$ almost surely exit the limiting
semicircle compact support as the size $N$ becomes large. The corresponding
limits are universal in the sense that they only involve the variance of the
entries of $W_N$. On the other hand, when $A_N$ is diagonal with a sole simple
nonnull eigenvalue large enough, we prove that the fluctuations of the largest
eigenvalue are not universal and vary with the particular distribution of the
entries of $W_N$.

To this aim, we first extend to the Wigner case a deformation method originally introduced for the GOE Tracy-Widom distribution. Then we study the statistics of $\lambda_N$ for a family of Wigner random matrices which shares some properties with Wigner matrices. We give a nonrigorous argument which suggests that the spectrum of this family of Wigner matrices converges in distribution to a deterministic parameter which we identify. We then present rigorous results which support this nonrigorous argument. In particular, we prove convergence in distribution of the spectrum of Wigner matrices with rank tending to infinity. Interestingly, we also show that this convergence result is nonuniversal: the fluctuations of the largest eigenvalue around its mean do not depend on the deterministic parameter. These findings are in sharp contrast with the GOE case where the Tracy-Widom distribution is universal.

Title:
The structure of hypersonic shock waves using Navier-Stokes equations modified to include mass diffusion.
Abstract:
human_text:
Howard Brenner has recently proposed modifications to the Navier-Stokes
equations that relate to a diffusion of fluid volume that would be significant
for flows with high density gradients. In a previous paper (Greenshields &
Reese, 2007), we found these modifications gave good predictions of the viscous
structure of shock waves in argon in the range Mach 1.0-12.0 (while
conventional Navier-Stokes equations are known to fail above about Mach 2).
However, some areas of concern with this model were a somewhat arbitrary choice
of modelling coefficient, and potentially unphysical and unstable solutions. In
this paper, we therefore present slightly different modifications to include
molecule mass diffusion fully in the Navier-Stokes equations. These
modifications are shown to be stable and produce physical solutions to the
shock problem of a quality broadly similar to those from the family of extended
hydrodynamic models that includes the Burnett equations. The modifications
primarily add a diffusion term to the mass conservation equation, so are at
least as simple to solve as the Navier-Stokes equations; there are none of the
numerical implementation problems of conventional extended hydrodynamics
models, particularly in respect of boundary conditions. We recommend further
investigation and testing on a number of different benchmark non-equilibrium
flow cases.
machine_text: Shock waves are a common phenomenon in the atmosphere, where they occur as brief periods of instability in the atmospheric pressure and density. They are characterized by a sharp gradient in these variables, and are often observed as sudden changes in hue and cloud patterns. At the speeds at which shock waves occur in the atmosphere (sonic velocities), hypersonic shock waves also affect the airframe of aircraft. These are typically caused by a combination of friction and compressibility effects, and are characterized by a sharp gradient in temperature and pressure as well as a transition in the chemical composition of the air. When used in high-speed flight, such airframe deformations can result in severe drag, increase in fuel consumption, and can lead to structural failure of the aircraft. In hypersonic flight, airframe deformation occurs on a much smaller time-scale than atmospheric variability. In response to these rapid changes, thermal effects become significant, as the airframe is capable of responding on shorter timescales than the thermal inertia of the fuel and passengers. In this sense, hypersonic flight differs from subsonic flight, which is characterized by low mass transport and slow thermal dynamics. Recent advances in computational fluid dynamics have enabled the accurate modeling of hypersonic shock waves, including thermal diffusion effects. We implement this approach in the incompressible Navier-Stokes equations, to model the shock wave in a qualitative manner. In particular, we investigate the effect of the Grashof and Sack Rosenbloom-Kempen tensor terms on the shock dynamics. These terms are normally negligible in the low Mach numbers of atmospheric flight, but they become dominant in hypersonic flows. In particular, we find that Grashof and Sack Rosenbloom-Kempen diffusion affect the strength of the shock and modify its characteristics compared to the classical shock. Our results demonstrate that the strength of hypersonic shock waves can be affected by thermal diffusion. In turn, this suggests that aerodynamic and structural characteristics of the shock wave can also be affected. Furthermore, the methods proposed in this work can be applied to other fields in aerodynamics, such as Laminar flow control and boundary layer control.

Title:
Nonequilibrium spin-dependent phenomena in mesoscopic superconductor-normal metal tunnel structures.
Abstract:
human_text:
We analyze the broad range of spin-dependent nonequilibrium transport
properties of hybrid systems composed of a normal region tunnel coupled to two
superconductors with exchange fields induced by the proximity to thin
ferromagnetic layers and highlight its functionalities. By calculating the
quasiparticle distribution functions in the normal region we find that they are
spin-dependent and strongly sensitive to the relative angle between exchange
fields in the two superconductors. The impact of inelastic collisions on their
properties is addressed. As a result, the electric current flowing through the
system is found to be strongly dependent on the relative angle between exchange
fields, giving rise to a huge value of magnetoresistance. Moreover, the current
presents a complete spin-polarization in a wide range of bias voltages, even in
the quasiequilibrium case. In the nonequilibrium limit we parametrize the
distributions with an ``effective`` temperature, which turns out to be strongly
spin-dependent, though quite sensitive to inelastic collisions. By tunnel
coupling the normal region to an additional superconducting electrode we show
that it is possible to implement a spin-polarized current source of both spin
species, depending on the bias voltages applied.
machine_text: We study theoretically spin-dependent transport properties of superconducting single-electron transistors (SSETs) connected in parallel to normal-metal electrodes. The conductance of each SSET as well as the total conductance of the structure depend on the relative orientation of the magnetic moments of the two SSETs and the spin polarization of the terminals. We analyze the influence of the phase differences between the superconductor leads on the magnetoconductance oscillations. We show that the structure exhibits a new kind of nonequilibrium magnetic response, which is based on the difference between the ferromagnetic and antiferromagnetic arrangements of the magnetic moments. The phenomenon is analogous to the exchange enhancement of magnetoresistance in magnetic heterostructures. We observe oscillations of the total conductance related to the flux quantum through the SSETs' Josephson junctions. The position and the amplitude of the peaks in the magnetic response as well as the period of the flux quantum oscillations depend on the phase differences between the superconductors. These results could be used to develop sensors based on magnetic superinductances using hybrid structures with SSETs.'

Title:
Quantum simulation of interacting high-dimensional systems: the influence of noise.
Abstract:
human_text:
We consider the simulation of interacting high-dimensional systems using
pairwise interacting qubits. The main tool in this context is the generation of
effective many-body interactions, and we examine a number of different
protocols for obtaining them. These methods include the usage of higher-order
processes (commutator method), unitary conjugation or graph state encoding, as
well as teleportation based approaches. We illustrate and compare these methods
in detail and analyze the time cost for simulation. In the second part of the
article, we investigate the influence of noise on the simulation process. We
concentrate on errors in the interaction Hamiltonians and consider two generic
noise models, (i) timing errors in pairwise interactions and (ii) noisy
pairwise interactions described by Master equations of Lindblad form. We
analyze and compare the effect of noise for the different simulation methods
and propose a way to significantly reduce the influence of noise by making use
of entanglement purification together with a teleportation based protocol.
machine_text: In this article, we simulate the quantum evolution of high-dimensional interaction Hamiltonians on a digital quantum simulator. We consider systems of up to 10^6^ spins, each evolving under a different short-range interaction term. While scalable quantum simulators must contend with both interactions and imperfections, we demonstrate that incorporating redirection gates can mitigate the effects of noise and extended evolution times relative to alternative simulation strategies. In particular, we simulate the dynamics of the Heisenberg model, the square-exchange model, and the random-exchange Ising model, all the way to their respective Néel temperatures. variant of the Heisenberg and square-exchange models have previously been simulated on noisy quantum computers with variational methods, where the effects of noise were not addressed. We also simulate the dynamics of the random-exchange Ising model, which has not previously been done in the quantum setting. We further demonstrate that noise may be exploited for quantum simulation, by simulating the dynamics of the Floquet time crystal model. Finally, we simulate the dynamics of time-evolving block decimation, a method for simulating renormalization group flows.

Title:
A Cross-disciplinary Framework for the Description of Contextually Mediated Change.
Abstract:
human_text:
We present a mathematical framework (referred to as Context-driven
Actualization of Potential, or CAP) for describing how entities change over
time under the influence of a context. The approach facilitates comparison of
change of state of entities studied in different disciplines. Processes are
seen to differ according to the degree of nondeterminism, and the degree to
which they are sensitive to, internalize, and depend upon a particular context.
Our analysis suggests that the dynamical evolution of a quantum entity
described by the Schrodinger equation is not fundamentally different from
change provoked by a measurement often referred to as collapse, but a limiting
case, with only one way to collapse. The biological transition to coded
replication is seen as a means of preserving structure in the fact of
context-driven change, and sextual replication as a means of increasing
potentiality thus enhancing diversity through interaction with context. The
framework sheds light on concepts like selection and fitness, reveals how
exceptional Darwinian evolution is as a means of 'change of state', and
clarifies in what sense culture, and the creative process underlying it, are
Darwinian.
machine_text: Contextual changes occur when the environment or the circumstances of a person or thing change, and the change affects or is affected by the person or thing's behavioral or structural characteristics. In the context of Technology, environmental changes may be driven by Technological progress, new regulations or legislation, new business models or customer needs, and new innovations. These changes may prompt different organizations or individuals to re-evaluate their position and approach, which may lead to Contextual Changes. In this article, we present an Organizational Change Framework to capture, categorize, and map these changes and their effects. Our framework comprises four layers: 1) People, 2) Processes, 3) Systems and 4) Context. At the People Layer, we define roles and responsibilities. At the Processes Layer, we describe the change management process. At the Systems Layer, we identify impacted systems and their capabilities. At the Context Layer, we map the affected context factors. By aggregating these four layers, we obtain a Contextual Change Description (CCD), which provides a comprehensive view of the change and its impact. We present use-case examples to illustrate how the framework can be applied to various types of changes.

Title:
Output Stream of Binding Neuron with Feedback.
Abstract:
human_text:
The binding neuron model is inspired by numerical simulation of
Hodgkin-Huxley-type point neuron, as well as by the leaky integrate-and-fire
model. In the binding neuron, the trace of an input is remembered for a fixed
period of time after which it disappears completely. This is in the contrast
with the above two models, where the postsynaptic potentials decay
exponentially and can be forgotten only after triggering. The finiteness of
memory in the binding neuron allows one to construct fast recurrent networks
for computer modeling. Recently, the finiteness is utilized for exact
mathematical description of the output stochastic process if the binding neuron
is driven with the Poissonian input stream. In this paper, the simplest
networking is considered for binding neuron. Namely, it is expected that every
output spike of single neuron is immediately fed into its input. For this
construction, externally fed with Poissonian stream, the output stream is
characterized in terms of interspike interval probability density distribution
if the binding neuron has threshold 2. For higher thresholds, the distribution
is calculated numerically. The distributions are compared with those found for
binding neuron without feedback, and for leaky integrator. Sample distributions
for leaky integrator with feedback are calculated numerically as well. It is
oncluded that even the simplest networking can radically alter spikng
statistics. Information condensation at the level of single neuron is
discussed.
machine_text: Neurons in the central nervous system transmit information by propagating action potentials, also known as “spikes”. These spikes initiate at the axon of a neuron, and then propagate along the axon to the terminal bulb, where they cause a change in membrane potential. This change in membrane potential subsequently leads to a change in membrane conductance, which causes a post-synaptic potential in target cells. This post-synaptic potential may then lead to a new spike in the target cell. This positive feedback loop is often called the neuron’s “wave”. Positive feedback is necessary for neurons to fire at high rates. However, not all neurons exhibit oscillatory behavior. For these neurons, the axon may ultimately repolarize below the threshold for spike initiation, leading to the cessation of the post-synaptic potential and the cessation of the spike. This type of negative feedback is known as “repolarization feedback”. Repolarization feedback has been observed in a variety of preparations, including locust giant Kenyon cell dendrites, lamprey spinal interneurons, and mammalian neocortical pyramidal neurons. Repolarization feedback has been shown to play a critical role in regulating the firing rates of neurons.

Title:
(An)isotropy of the Hubble diagram: comparing hemispheres.
Abstract:
human_text:
We test the isotropy of the Hubble diagram. At small redshifts, this is
possible without assumptions on the cosmic inventory and provides a fundamental
test of the cosmological principle. At higher redshift we check for the
self-consistency of the LambdaCDM model. At small redshifts, we use public
supernovae (SNe) Ia data to determine the deceleration parameter q_0 and the SN
calibration on opposite hemispheres. For the complete data sets we fit Omega_M
and the SN calibration on opposite hemispheres. A statistically significant
anisotropy of the Hubble diagram at redshifts z < 0.2 is discovered (> 95%
C.L.). While data from the North Galactic hemisphere favour the accelerated
expansion of the Universe, data from the South Galactic hemisphere are not
conclusive. The hemispheric asymmetry is maximal toward a direction close to
the equatorial poles. The discrepancy between the equatorial North and South
hemispheres shows up in the SN calibration. For the LambdaCDM model fitted to
all available SNe, we find the same asymmetry. The alignment of discrepancies
between hemispheric Hubble diagrams with the equatorial frame seems to point
toward a systematic error in the SN search, observation, analysis or data
reduction. We also find that our model independent test cannot exclude the case
of the deceleration of the expansion at a statistically significant level.
machine_text: A long-standing problem in cosmology is to explain the observed isotropy of the sky. One of the main arguments against an early period of anisotropy is the relatively low degree of isotropy on scales of the order of the size of the Earth's orbit about the sun (i.e., approximately 30 degrees). In recent years, several groups have claimed to observe higher degrees of anisotropy on smaller scales. These include, for example, regions of the sky devoid of galaxies and quasars, high-density regions within large-scale voids, and the entire gravitational wave horizon. In this work, we perform a direct, all-sky comparison of the Hubble diagrams of the northern and southern hemispheres. We compute the ratio of the distances to galaxies (i.e., the Hubble parameter) separately for each hemisphere and find no significant evidence for anisotropy. The best-fit amplitude of anisotropy, as determined from our analysis, is |2%|, which is consistent with the currently observed sensitivities of measurements of anisotropy on large angular scales.

Title:
A CLT for Information-theoretic statistics of Gram random matrices with a given variance profile.
Abstract:
human_text:
Consider a $N\times n$ random matrix $Y_n=(Y_{ij}^{n})$ where the entries are
given by $$ Y_{ij}^{n}=\frac{\sigma_{ij}(n)}{\sqrt{n}} X_{ij}^{n} $$ the
$X_{ij}^{n}$ being centered, independent and identically distributed random
variables with unit variance and $(\sigma_{ij}(n); 1\le i\le N, 1\le j\le n)$
being an array of numbers we shall refer to as a variance profile. We study in
this article the fluctuations of the random variable $$ \log\det(Y_n Y_n^* +
\rho I_N) $$ where $Y^*$ is the Hermitian adjoint of $Y$ and $\rho > 0$ is an
additional parameter. We prove that when centered and properly rescaled, this
random variable satisfies a Central Limit Theorem (CLT) and has a Gaussian
limit whose parameters are identified. A complete description of the scaling
parameter is given; in particular it is shown that an additional term appears
in this parameter in the case where the 4$^\textrm{th}$ moment of the
$X_{ij}$'s differs from the 4$^{\textrm{th}}$ moment of a Gaussian random
variable. Such a CLT is of interest in the field of wireless communications.
machine_text: A general central limit theorem is proved for the information-theoretic statistics of Gram random matrices with a given variance profile. The result applies, in particular, to the standard parametric and nonparametric estimation of the scalar variance and the mean of a multivariate normal distribution. In the former case, the scalar variance is always estimated unbiasedly while the mean is estimated unbiasedly only when all the variances are estimated to be 1. The Gaussian variance profile models are carefully compared to the Laplace and the double-factor models. Numerical experiments on practical classification problems consistently confirm the superior performance of the variance profile estimation over the conventional mean estimation, which justifies the recently gained popularity of the information-theoretic criterion in machine learning and statistics. The result is a direct corollary of a more general uniform distributional convergence in the large Gram matrix size limit, which is of independent interest and may have other applications.

Title:
Kullback-Leibler distance as a measure of the information filtered from multivariate data.
Abstract:
human_text:
We show that the Kullback-Leibler distance is a good measure of the
statistical uncertainty of correlation matrices estimated by using a finite set
of data. For correlation matrices of multivariate Gaussian variables we
analytically determine the expected values of the Kullback-Leibler distance of
a sample correlation matrix from a reference model and we show that the
expected values are known also when the specific model is unknown. We propose
to make use of the Kullback-Leibler distance to estimate the information
extracted from a correlation matrix by correlation filtering procedures. We
also show how to use this distance to measure the stability of filtering
procedures with respect to statistical uncertainty. We explain the
effectiveness of our method by comparing four filtering procedures, two of them
being based on spectral analysis and the other two on hierarchical clustering.
We compare these techniques as applied both to simulations of factor models and
empirical data. We investigate the ability of these filtering procedures in
recovering the correlation matrix of models from simulations. We discuss such
an ability in terms of both the heterogeneity of model parameters and the
length of data series. We also show that the two spectral techniques are
typically more informative about the sample correlation matrix than techniques
based on hierarchical clustering, whereas the latter are more stable with
respect to statistical uncertainty.
machine_text: Information theoretic measures have been widely used in Statistics and Information Theory to quantify the amount of information contained in a given distribution. In this work we show that the Kullback-Leibler divergence can be used to measure the amount of information filtered from multivariate data by a given statistical model. This provides a link between two widely used families of Information Theory measures, namely those derived from the approximation theory and those derived from the Fisher discrimination theory. We illustrate the usefulness of this approach by applying it to describe how the amount of information of a multivariate Gaussian distribution is affected by model parameters, such as its mean and covariance matrix. We show that the Kullback-Leibler divergence can be used to characterize how much the observed data have been deviated from Gaussianity. Such deviation is quantified in terms of the error rate of the maximum likelihood estimator, the divergence always being non-negative. We also discuss the relations with the Cramer-Rao and Rissanou inequalities. We provide some explicit examples for the Gaussian case, as well as a comparison with the mean squared error of the maximum likelihood estimator. We illustrate the usefulness of this framework to characterize the information contained in macroeconomic time series, such as inflation and GDP.

Title:
The geometrical quantity in damped wave equations on a square.
Abstract:
human_text:
The energy in a square membrane $\Omega$ subject to constant viscous damping
on a subset $\omega\subset \Omega$ decays exponentially in time as soon as
$\omega$ satisfies a geometrical condition known as the "Bardos-Lebeau-Rauch"
condition. The rate $\tau(\omega)$ of this decay satisfies $\tau(\omega)= 2
\min(-\mu(\omega), g(\omega))$ (see Lebeau [Math. Phys. Stud. 19 (1996)
73-109]). Here $\mu(\omega)$ denotes the spectral abscissa of the damped wave
equation operator and $g(\omega)$ is a number called the geometrical quantity
of $\omega$ and defined as follows. A ray in $\Omega$ is the trajectory
generated by the free motion of a mass-point in $\Omega$ subject to elastic
reflections on the boundary. These reflections obey the law of geometrical
optics. The geometrical quantity $g(\omega)$ is then defined as the upper limit
(large time asymptotics) of the average trajectory length. We give here an
algorithm to compute explicitly $g(\omega)$ when $\omega$ is a finite union of
squares.
machine_text: In this paper, we consider a one-dimensional damped wave equation in a square. We show that the longitudinal strain energy density, which is the metric in elasticity theory, is a geometrical quantity that satisfies the damped wave equation. The longitudinal strain energy density has been used to characterize the mode I and mode II transversal vibration of a plate. We find the formulas to compute the longitudinal strain energy density at a point in the square based on the value at neighboring points. The solution of the damped wave equation indicates that the longitudinal strain energy density decreases in time like an exponential. We also show that the area strain energy density, which is the metric in Fluid theory, is a geometrical quantity that satisfies the damped wave equation. The area strain energy density has been used to describe the irrotational flow of a fluid. We also find the solution of the damped wave equation and find that the area strain energy density decreases in time like an exponential.

Title:
Entropy signature of the running cosmological constant.
Abstract:
human_text:
Renormalization group (RG) improved cosmologies based upon a RG trajectory of
Quantum Einstein Gravity (QEG) with realistic parameter values are investigated
using a system of cosmological evolution equations which allows for an
unrestricted energy exchange between the vacuum and the matter sector. It is
demonstrated that the scale dependence of the gravitational parameters, the
cosmological constant in particular, leads to an entropy production in the
matter system. The picture emerges that the Universe started out from a state
of vanishing entropy, and that the radiation entropy observed today is
essentially due to the coarse graining (RG flow) in the quantum gravity sector
which is related to the expansion of the Universe. Furthermore, the RG improved
field equations are shown to possess solutions with an epoch of power law
inflation immediately after the initial singularity. The inflation is driven by
the cosmological constant and ends automatically once the RG running has
reduced the vacuum energy to the level of the matter energy density.
machine_text: We present a novel approach to probing the space-time geometry using the statistical properties of the observed structures in the universe. Using the redshift-temperature relation of the cosmic microwave background (CMB) and the distortion information from the Integrated Sachs-Wolfe (ISW) effect, we construct the so-called "entropy-temperature" plane. We show that the cosmological constant, which is believed to drive the current expansion of the universe, affects the theoretical predictions in this plane in a distinct manner from various dark energy candidates. As an example, we apply our method to the latest observed Sloan Digital Sky Survey (SDSS) data and put a tight constraint on the space-time curvature tensor in the universe. Using the full galaxy sample, our analysis improves the constraint on the non-flat universe from the previous result by Anderson et al. (2013) by more than a factor of two. We forecast that the forthcoming results from the completed SDSS-III BOSS survey will further improve the constraint on the curvature parameters.

Title:

Abstract:
human_text:
Theoretical research on electronic properties in mesoscopic condensed matter
systems has focused primarily on the electron charge freedom degrees, while its
corresponding spin freedom degrees have not yet received the same attention.
Nevertheless nowadays there has been an increment in the number of electron
spin-related experiments showing unique possibilities for finding novel
mechanisms of information processing and transmission, opening ample fields of
opportunities in the theoretical developed of new models. In this spirit we
have calculated the resonant tunneling characteristics curves in double-barrier
heterostructures of GaAs-Ga1-x AlxAs under external stress and considering two
charges with spin half. The resonant tunneling study has been carried out by
means of the diagrammatic techniques for non equilibrium processes following
the model proposed by Keldysh also a simple one-band tight-binding Hamiltonian
is adopted in the theoretical framework. We have compared our results of the
spin-tunneling with previous ones reported in literature.
machine_text: The spin-dependent resonant tunneling characteristics of a double-barrier heterostructures under longitudinal stresses are theoretically investigated based on a 3D effective mass model. The stress-dependent band gaps and Dresselhaus coupling strength are employed to describe the spin-dependent band structures. The theoretical results show that the spin-dependent resonant tunneling probability is highly sensitive to the longitudinal stresses, and two stress-induced resonance peaks can be clearly observed for a positive longitudinal stress, which can be effectively utilized in the device application. Moreover, the symmetry properties of the longitudinal stress-dependent resonant tunneling characteristics are studied in detail. The theoretical results provide a feasible route to explore the spin-dependent transport properties and may be helpful for designing the stress-sensitive resonant tunneling devices. Title:
Regge approach to charged-pion photoproduction at invariant energies above 2 GeV.
Abstract:
human_text:
A Regge model with absorptive corrections is employed in a global analysis of
the world data on positive and negative pion photoproduction for photon
energies from 3 to 8 GeV. In this region resonance contributions are expected
to be negligible so that the available experimental information on differential
cross sections and single polarization observables at -t \leq 2 GeV^2 allows us
to determine the non-resonant part of the reaction amplitude reliably. The
model amplitude is then used to predict observables for photon energies below 3
GeV. Differences between our predictions and data in this energy region are
systematically examined as possible signals for the presence of excited
baryons. We find that the data available for the polarized photon asymmetry
show promising resonance signatures at invariant energies around 2 GeV. With
regard to differential cross sections the analysis of negative pion
photoproduction data, obtained recently at JLab, indicates likewise the
presence of resonance structures around 2 GeV
machine_text: In this paper we review the general formalism and apply it to charged-pion photoproduction reactions at energies above the two-pion threshold, i.e. at invariant energies greater than 2 GeV. First, we present a spin-averaged amplitude, based on a Lagrangian that includes nucleons, resonances, and hyperons as explicit degrees of freedom. The excitation spectrum of the latter is consistent with the most recent experimental findings. To this we add a phenomenological Lagrangian that accounts for the known tensor-force component in the $t$-channel exchanges. Next, using the principle of maximum optical rigidity, we fix the couplings of the resonances to the known states. We consider not only the well-established excited states, but also many resonances that have been proposed in the recent literature. We show that the large-$N_c$ approximation is violated for the exchange of the Roper and theDelta resonances. We perform a systematic study of the resonance parameters and their interference with the background contributions, in order to reproduce the existing photoproduction data above 2 GeV. The results for the amplitudes are provided as computer code.

Title:
Pressure induced Insulator-Metal transition in LaMnO$_3$.
Abstract:
human_text:
The recent observation of a insulator to metal transition (IMT) [I. Loa et
al, PRL 87, 125501 (2001)] in pure LaMnO$_3$ at 32 GPa and room temperature,
well above the Neel temperature (145 K) and below the Jahn-Teller transition
temperature (780 K), opens the way to a study of the role of the orbital
degrees of freedom on the electronic structure in a stoichiometric material. In
this paper we focus our attention in the orbital aspects of the insulator to
metal transition. We use a model Hamiltonian for the $e_g$ orbitals of Mn that
includes the on site Coulomb repulsion $U$, the hopping $t$, and its dependence
with pressure. In order to include in an appropriate way the strong
correlations induced by the dominant electron-electron interactions we
introduce auxiliary fields (Slave Bosons,SB) to the description of the low
energy states. We use a O-Mn distance ($d$) dependence of $t$ and the
pressure-$d$ relation from the experimental data to describe the evolution of
the electronic structure with pressure. Our results confirm and make
transparent the conclusion reached in previous ab-initio calculations: the
inclusion of the Coulomb energy is necessary and constitutes an important
factor enhancing the orbital polarization in these compounds.

Studies on polycrystalline specimen of LaMnO$_3$ up to 23 GPa show significant distortion of the MnO6 octahedra as evident from synchrotron X-ray spectroscopy. Resistance studies on LaMnO3 show semiconductor like behavior up to 12 GPa and formation of metallic like conduction at higher pressures (15-23 GPa). Resistivity exhibits metal to insulator transition around 11 GPa where a kink appears in the plot. This is accompanied by change in behavior of magnetic susceptibility from ferromagnetic to canted ferromagnetic state.
